articles.title: A six-digit code in the inbox does not mean email verification works
articles.description: An end-to-end test requests an email code, finds six digits in a message, enters them, and sees a green checkmark. It proves that one code can complete one path. It says nothing about whether an expired code still works, a resend leaves two valid codes behind, or the same code can be replayed. That gap matters because email OTP verification is a small state machine. Tests should cover the transitions and the boundaries around them, not just the happy path. Start with a behavior table Before writing selectors, write down what the product promises. A useful minimum looks like this: Situation Expected result Correct, unexpired code Verification succeeds for the address that requested it Incorrect code Verification stays incomplete; a clear error appears Expired code Verification is rejected Code submitted twice The second submission is rejected if codes are single-use Resend requested The newest message arrives; behavior of the older code matches the product's policy Delivery delayed or missing The test fails with a useful timeout, not a fixed sleep or a false pass The last detail in the resend row is a product decision. Some systems invalidate the previous code on resend; others allow both until their individual expiry. Make the contract explicit, then assert that contract. Give every run its own recipient Parallel tests that share an email address can read one another's messages. A unique recipient per test run gives the test a reliable way to isolate delivery. Use a new address for retries too, so a delayed email from a failed attempt cannot be mistaken for the retry's code. Create the inbox before triggering the send. Then wait for a message with the sender or subject you expect. A real wait for a matching message is better than waitForTimeout(5000): a sleep is sometimes too short and otherwise makes every run slower. Here is the delivery portion using Playwright's request client and an InboxRhino inbox fixture. The fixture should provide a ready inbox and delete it after each test. Keep the API key in the test runner's environment or CI secrets. import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test'; test('verifies an address using the code delivered to this run', async ({ page, request, inbox }) => { await page.goto('https://staging.example.com/verify-email'); await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(inbox.address); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send code' }).click(); expect(response.status()).toBe(200); const { data } = await response.json(); expect(data).toHaveLength(1); expect(data[0].to.toLowerCase()).toBe(inbox.address.toLowerCase()); expect(match, 'message should contain a code in the expected template').not.toBeNull(); await page.getByLabel('Verification code').fill(match![1]); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Verify' }).click(); await expect(page.getByTestId('verified-email')).toHaveText(inbox.address); }); The subject, sender, message template, page selectors, and fixture are examples; replace them with your application's contract. Avoid extracting the first six digits from any message. It might be a support number, an order ID, or a code from a different notification. Assert the recipient too, and make the UI show which address became verified. Test expiry without relying on the wall clock Waiting around for a production-length expiry makes a slow and flaky test. If the application has an injectable clock or a test-only expiry setting, issue a code, advance time past its expiry, and submit it. Assert that verification is rejected and the account remains unverified. Keep that test seam restricted to the test environment. If the app has no controllable clock, test the expired-code branch at the service boundary with a fixed clock, then keep one shorter end-to-end test to prove the actual email and UI path work together. Treat resend as a separate transition Resend behavior catches subtle defects: the second email never arrives, the interface reports success when sending failed, or an older code remains valid against a policy that says it should be revoked. Use the same inbox for a resend test only when the inbox query can distinguish the messages reliably. Capture message identifiers or a delivery timestamp, request the resend, and wait for the next matching message. Then assert the old and new code behavior according to the documented policy. Do not assume that a later received_at proves which UI action caused the message; a delayed message from the earlier request can arrive later. Check the account state, not just the response text “Code accepted” is a weak final assertion if the verification page can accept a code for the wrong account. Assert the email address displayed as verified, or check persisted account state through a test-only API. For single-use codes, submit the same code again and assert it is rejected. For wrong-code handling, check that the account remains unverified as well as checking the visible error. Keep OTPs and full email bodies out of CI logs. Record safer diagnostics such as the recipient, message ID, test-run ID, and whether the verification state changed. Never put a real user's mailbox or production account into an end-to-end test. The goal is not to test every combination of digits. It is to test the small number of state transitions that define the security and user experience of the flow. Once those expectations are written down, the inbox becomes one step in a precise test, rather than a six-digit string that happens to make the suite green. Disclosure: I build InboxRhino, a receive-only inbox API for email tests. The state-machine checks here apply with any test mailbox your runner can read.

articles.title: How ML Models Are Actually Trained: A Beginner’s Guide to the Frontier
articles.description: TL;DR: You almost never need to pre-train a model. The economical path for small teams and researchers is to take a strong open base model → fine-tune it cheaply (LoRA/QLoRA) on your high-quality data → or skip training entirely and use RAG. Pre-training from scratch is for the few labs with nine-figure budgets. This is a conceptual + strategic guide. It covers: How machine-learning models (especially large language models) are actually trained. How to make training economical. How the Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Kimi/Moonshot, Qwen/Alibaba) train differently from the Western frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, Google/Gemini). How all of those differ from agentic tools like Kiro. Where specialized research projects (like NeuroJen) sit on that spectrum. How the Prima Mente Alzheimer's Translation Challenge relates to this ecosystem. Facts about third-party models were verified against public sources (technical reports, model cards, vendor docs) as of October 2026. The field moves fast; treat version-specific numbers as "accurate at time of writing." How ML models are trained (the fundamentals) The LLM training pipeline, stage by stage What training actually costs — and how to make it economical The Chinese labs: DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen The Western frontier labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google How they differ — a side-by-side Where Kiro fits (it isn't a model maker) Where specialized projects fit The Prima Mente Alzheimer's Translation Challenge How the challenge relates to this project Glossary 1. How ML models are trained At its core, "training" a model means adjusting millions-to-trillions of numbers (parameters/weights) so the model's predictions get closer to the right answers. The loop is always the same: 1. Forward pass — Feed input in, model produces an output (a prediction). 2. Loss — Compare the prediction to the desired answer; compute an error number ("loss"). Lower = better. 3. Backward pass — "Backpropagation": compute how each weight contributed to the error (the gradient). 4. Update — Nudge each weight slightly in the direction that reduces the loss (an "optimizer" like AdamW does this). 5. Repeat — Millions of times over billions of examples. A few ideas that matter for everything below: Parameters (weights): The model's learned knowledge. "A 7B model" = 7 billion parameters. More parameters ≈ more capacity, but also more compute and memory. Tokens: Text is chopped into tokens (~¾ of a word each). Models are trained on trillions of tokens. "14.8T tokens" means 14.8 trillion. Compute: Measured in GPU-hours or FLOPs. This is the dominant cost. The scaling laws: Empirically, performance improves predictably as you scale model size, data, and compute together. This is why frontier models got huge. But bigger is not automatically better per dollar — which is the whole story of Sections 3–4. 2. The LLM training pipeline Modern large language models are built in phases, each with a different purpose: Phase A — Pre-training (the expensive one) The model reads a vast corpus (web text, books, code — trillions of tokens) and learns to predict the next token. This is self-supervised: no human labels needed, the "answer" is just the next word in the text. This phase creates a base model that has broad knowledge but isn't yet helpful or safe. It consumes ~95%+ of the total training compute. Phase B — Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) / instruction tuning The base model is trained on curated input→output pairs (e.g. "Question → good answer", "Instruction → correct completion"). This teaches it to follow instructions and respond in a useful format. Much cheaper than pre-training — thousands to millions of examples, not trillions of tokens. Phase C — Alignment / preference optimization Make the model helpful, honest, and harmless. Techniques: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): Humans rank answers; a reward model learns their preferences; the LLM is optimized against it (classically with PPO). DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): A simpler, cheaper alternative to RLHF that skips the separate reward model. Constitutional AI (Anthropic): The model critiques/revises its own answers against a written set of principles ("a constitution"), reducing the human-labeling burden. Phase D — Reasoning training (the 2024–2026 shift) Teach the model to "think" before answering — produce a long chain-of-thought, then the final answer. This is often done with reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards (e.g. math/code problems where correctness is checkable). DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI's "o" series popularized this. It dramatically improves hard reasoning without making the base model bigger. 3. What training costs Why it's expensive Frontier pre-training needs thousands of top-tier GPUs running for months. A single frontier run can cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in compute alone — plus data, salaries, and failed runs. This is why only a handful of organizations pre-train frontier models from scratch. The levers that make training economical Lever What it does Who uses it Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Only activate a subset of the network per token (e.g. 37B of 671B). Huge capacity, fraction of the compute per token. DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, Mixtral Low precision (FP8/INT4) Train/run in 8-bit (or 4-bit) instead of 16/32-bit → less memory, faster math. DeepSeek (FP8 pre-training), most quantized inference Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) Freeze the base model; train tiny "adapter" matrices (~0.1–1% of weights). Fine-tune a big model on one GPU. Most open-source fine-tuning, specialized research Quantization Store weights in 4-bit for inference/training → fits bigger models on smaller GPUs. QLoRA, llama.cpp, Unsloth Distillation Train a small "student" model to imitate a big "teacher". Cheap models that punch above their size. DeepSeek-R1-Distill, many small models Better optimizers / stability tricks Converge faster / avoid wasteful failed runs (e.g. Muon, MuonClip). Kimi K2 (MuonClip) Data quality over quantity Clean, de-duplicated, well-curated data trains better per token. Everyone serious about results Retrieval (RAG) instead of training Put knowledge in a searchable store and retrieve it at query time rather than baking it into weights. Near-zero training cost. Most production deployments Free/cheap compute tiers Kaggle (free T4 GPUs 30h/wk), Colab, Modal credits, spot instances. Students, small teams, researchers The single most important beginner lesson You almost never need to pre-train. The economical path is: take a strong open base model → fine-tune it cheaply (LoRA/QLoRA) on your high-quality data → or skip training entirely and use RAG. Pre-training from scratch is for the few labs with nine-figure budgets. Everyone else builds on top. 4. The Chinese labs The defining theme of the Chinese frontier labs is efficiency and openness — achieving near-frontier quality at a fraction of the reported cost, and releasing open weights (you can download and run the model yourself). DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V3 / R1) Architecture: Mixture-of-Experts — 671B total parameters, ~37B active per token. You get the capacity of a huge model at the compute of a ~37B one. Scale & cost: Pre-trained on 14.8 trillion tokens using FP8 (8-bit) training, in ~2.788 million H800 GPU-hours. The widely-cited figure is a ~$5.6M compute cost for the main run — one to two orders of magnitude below typical Western frontier estimates. (Caveat: this is the final run's compute, not total R&D, and the comparison is imperfect — but the efficiency is real.) R1 (reasoning): Trained reasoning ability largely through reinforcement learning (GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization). Famously, R1-Zero was trained with RL and no supervised cold-start, showing reasoning can emerge from RL alone; the shipped R1 adds a small SFT cold-start for readability. Openness: Open weights under a permissive (MIT) license; detailed technical reports. This is the opposite of the closed Western approach. Kimi (Moonshot AI — Kimi K2) Architecture: MoE — 1 trillion total parameters, ~32B active; 384 experts, 8 active per token. Training innovation: The MuonClip optimizer — the Muon optimizer plus a "QK-clip" technique to keep training stable at trillion-parameter scale (training instabilities are a major hidden cost; fixing them saves wasted runs). Focus: Agentic tool-use — built to call tools and act, not just chat. Notably, base K2 is not a chain-of-thought reasoning model by default; it's optimized for fast agentic action. Openness: Open weights. Qwen (Alibaba — Qwen3 family) A broad open-weight family: dense models (every parameter active) and MoE variants, across many sizes (small enough for a laptop up to very large). Strong on multilingual, coding, and agentic tasks; widely used as a base for downstream fine-tuning because of the permissive licensing and size range. The common thread MoE for efficiency + low-precision training + open weights + published methods. The strategic bet: openness drives adoption, and efficiency makes frontier-ish capability affordable. 5. The Western frontier labs OpenAI (GPT series) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only. Pioneered the modern RLHF-aligned assistant (InstructGPT → ChatGPT) and the reasoning-model wave (the "o" series). Very large (undisclosed) training budgets; strong product/ecosystem integration. Anthropic (Claude) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only. Known for Constitutional AI (aligning the model against a written set of principles with less human labeling) and a strong safety/reliability emphasis — which is why Claude is a popular default for agentic coding (it holds intent across long, multi-step tasks). Google (Gemini) Proprietary, closed weights, API-only, deeply multimodal (text, images, audio, video) and integrated across Google's products. Backed by Google's own TPU hardware and enormous data/compute. Important nuance: Google also publishes the open-weight Gemma family (including the medical MedGemma that many research projects build on). So "Google" spans both closed frontier (Gemini) and open small models (Gemma). Closed weights, API access, large undisclosed budgets, heavy investment in alignment and safety, and productization. You rent capability through an API rather than owning the model. 6. How they differ Dimension Chinese labs (DeepSeek/Kimi/Qwen) Western frontier (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google) Weights Open — download & self-host Closed — API only (except Google's Gemma) Headline strategy Efficiency + openness Capability + product + safety, kept proprietary Architecture trend Aggressive MoE (sparse) Mix; often undisclosed Training precision FP8 pre-training (DeepSeek) Undisclosed; generally higher precision historically Reported cost Dramatically lower (e.g. DeepSeek ~$5.6M run) Much higher (tens–hundreds of $M), undisclosed Reasoning RL-centric (GRPO; R1-Zero showed RL-only works) RLHF + dedicated reasoning models (o-series) Alignment Lighter / varies Heavy (RLHF, Constitutional AI, red-teaming) You can fine-tune it? Yes (open weights) No (closed) — you can only prompt/call it Transparency Detailed technical reports Limited; cards + marketing The practical upshot for a small team: Open-weight Chinese (and Google Gemma) models are the ones you can actually download, fine-tune, and own. Closed Western models are things you call. 7. Where Kiro fits Kiro is not a model maker — it's an agentic development tool (an IDE and CLI). This is a common point of confusion, so it's worth stating plainly: Kiro does not train its own foundation models. It runs on Amazon Bedrock and gives you access to other people's models: Anthropic's Claude (its historical default), OpenAI's GPT tiers, and open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen. Its "Auto" mode is a router: it picks the best available model for a given task based on complexity, latency, and cost. That orchestration — plus spec-driven workflows, tools, and a graph-based state engine — is Kiro's value-add, not the model weights. So on our map: the labs in Sections 4–5 make the models; Kiro orchestrates them. Model makers (train) Orchestrators (route+act) Domain fine-tuners (specialize) OpenAI, Anthropic, Kiro (agentic IDE/CLI on Specialized research (e.g. Google, DeepSeek, → Bedrock; routes to Claude/ → MedGemma + LoRA on Moonshot, Alibaba GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen via "Auto") curated scientific data) 8. Where specialized projects fit Specialized research projects (like NeuroJen) sit deliberately at the economical, specialized end of everything above. Base model: MedGemma-4B (a medical-domain model in Google's open Gemma family) — small, open, and already medically literate. Not pre-trained by us. Method: LoRA supervised fine-tuning via Unsloth, on a single free Kaggle T4 GPU (4-bit quantized). This is Section 3's economical toolkit applied end to end: open base + PEFT + quantization + free compute. The novelty — "answer-withholding" tasks: The training signal hides the field we want the model to predict, so it must reason about the body-to-brain link rather than reformat text. Stage 1 before any training — GraphRAG: Retrieval over a Neo4j knowledge graph, which gives value with zero GPU cost and acts as the baseline the fine-tuned model must beat. Honest evaluation: The fine-tuned model is actually queried and judged by an LLM-judge rubric. In one sentence: Where DeepSeek/OpenAI/etc. spend millions to pre-train general models, specialized projects spend ~$0 to specialize an existing open model for one disease — exactly the right strategy for a small research team. We are a consumer and specializer of the ecosystem, not a frontier trainer. 9. The Prima Mente Challenge Prima Mente is an AI-biology company (London/San Francisco) building epigenomic foundation models — large models trained on how genes are switched on/off across cell types (their model line is called Pleiades). They won the $1M ADDI Alzheimer's Insights AI Prize, connecting them directly to the AD Data Initiative ecosystem. The Alzheimer's Translation Challenge A global, free AI competition to find new therapeutic hypotheses for Alzheimer's, run with the Alzheimer's Disease Data Initiative (ADDI) and partners (NVIDIA, Hugging Face, Nebius, Prime Intellect, Goodfire, Boltz, and more). The data: A brand-new open-source cellular atlas of ~150 million cells — neurons, astrocytes, and microglia. Released in batches, accessed via AD Workbench and Prima Mente's modelling platform. Two stages: Stage 1 (build & evaluate): Every participant builds AI models on the atlas, assessed on a curated set of evals — general benchmarks, harder tasks such as phenocopy (predicting whether a perturbation reproduces a disease-like cell state), and community-proposed evals. Strongest results are shortlisted. Stage 2 (hypothesize & validate): Shortlisted participants each propose one new therapeutic hypothesis with its anticipated molecular/functional phenotypes. Finalists' hypotheses are tested in Prima Mente's wet lab — closing the loop "from biology to target to function." Timeline (as published): When Milestone October 2026 Registration opens (atlas generation underway) November 2026 Community launches (Q&A, teammates) December 2026 Prizes announced Spring 2027 Competition starts (dataset released; model-building + evals) Summer 2027 Hypothesis validation (finalists' hypotheses tested in the wet lab) Key terms: Free to enter; open to anyone (no biology background required — "set up so ML researchers can take part"); Prima Mente takes no rights to your model or discoveries; you may suggest a gene/compound to test at registration. 10. How the challenge relates to this project This is the strategically important part. Specialized projects and the Prima Mente challenge are complementary layers of the same translational-research stack, and the challenge is a natural proving ground for this thesis. The connection in one picture POPULATION / LITERATURE LAYER CELLULAR / MECHANISM LAYER Specialized Project Prima Mente challenge Mines papers → extracts structured 150M-cell atlas (neurons, astrocytes, "peripheral factor → mechanism → microglia) → model perturbations → central pathology" hypotheses phenocopy / therapeutic hypotheses \ / ▼ ▼ A testable hypothesis from the literature becomes a perturbation to evaluate in cells, and (if shortlisted) in Prima Mente's wet lab. Concrete ways they connect Hypothesis generation vs. validation: The specialized project generates hypotheses about the body-to-brain axis. The challenge is literally a hypothesis-validation engine (Stage 2 → wet lab). A finding like "chronic gut inflammation → gut-brain signalling → microglial activation in the hippocampus" is exactly the kind of specific, testable claim the challenge asks for — and the atlas contains hippocampal microglia to test it against. Shared infrastructure (AD Workbench): The challenge data is served through the AD Workbench — the same ADDI cloud environment researchers are applying to use. Work done for one directly builds capability for the other. Shared ecosystem partner (Hugging Face): Hugging Face is a challenge partner and the standard hub for models/datasets. The tooling overlaps significantly. "Translation" is the shared mission: The challenge is named the Translation Challenge because it moves insights from computation to lab-validated biology — which is precisely the "body-to-brain" aim, one layer up (literature) from Prima Mente's layer (single-cell). The register-a-perturbation hook: At registration you can submit a gene or compound you'd like tested. The structured hypotheses produced by the literature-mining front end are a ready-made source of candidate perturbations to propose — turning output directly into challenge input. Why this matters for the roadmap Participating (or at least aligning with the challenge) gives: A concrete downstream validation path for hypotheses (otherwise they're just text). Access to cellular-level data that complements literature-level data. Free compute and a community (NVIDIA/Nebius/Prime Intellect credits via the challenge). A credible, deadline-driven milestone (Spring 2027) to aim the pipeline at. Bottom line: The literature-mining front end and the cellular-and-wet-lab back end are two halves of the same "from papers to validated targets" pipeline. 11. Glossary Term Plain meaning Parameter / weight One of the many numbers a model learns. More = more capacity + cost. Token A chunk of text (~¾ word) the model reads/produces. Pre-training The big, expensive phase: learn language by predicting the next token on trillions of tokens. SFT Supervised Fine-Tuning: teach a base model to follow instructions with input→output pairs. RLHF Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: align a model to human preferences. DPO Direct Preference Optimization: a simpler, cheaper RLHF alternative. Constitutional AI Anthropic's method: the model self-critiques against written principles. MoE Mixture-of-Experts: activate only a subset of the network per token → big capacity, low per-token compute. LoRA / QLoRA Train tiny adapter weights (optionally on a 4-bit model) instead of the whole model → cheap fine-tuning. Store/run weights in fewer bits (FP8/INT4) → less memory, faster, cheaper. Train a small "student" to imitate a big "teacher". GRPO Group Relative Policy Optimization — the RL method behind DeepSeek-R1's reasoning. MuonClip Kimi K2's optimizer (Muon + QK-clip) for stable trillion-parameter training. RAG / GraphRAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch knowledge at query time instead of baking it into weights (GraphRAG uses a knowledge graph). Open vs closed weights Open = you can download & fine-tune the model; closed = API access only. Base vs instruct model Base = raw pre-trained; instruct = after SFT/alignment, ready to follow instructions. Phenocopy When a perturbation makes a cell look/behave like it has a disease — a key challenge eval.

articles.title: Our Newest Lorries Update Their Own Software Overnight and Nobody in My Department Approves It
articles.description: Of our seventy lorries, the twelve delivered this year are the first that receive software updates from their manufacturer over the mobile network. Software in a modern lorry manages the engine, the gearbox, the braking systems and the driver's displays. Until now it changed only when a lorry went into a workshop, where a technician connected a laptop and a fitter signed the job sheet. A United Nations regulation on vehicle software updates, known as R156 and adopted for new vehicles across Europe, requires manufacturers to manage updates as a controlled process. It covers updates sent over the air, makes sure an update can be installed safely, and requires the driver to be told what it will change. That is reassuring about the manufacturer. It says nothing about us. In September two of the new lorries installed an update overnight in our yard. The next morning the dashboard showed a new warning message, which the release notes described as a change to how tyre pressure readings are displayed. The release notes had been posted to the manufacturer's fleet portal, which nobody in our transport office signed in to. One driver rang in thinking his lorry was faulty and waited forty minutes for an answer. No harm was done. It was simply the first time a supplier had changed the behaviour of our equipment, on our premises, without anyone in the company knowing it was going to happen. For twenty years my department has managed software on things that stay in buildings. Our fleet is becoming a set of computers on wheels, changed by someone else on a schedule they choose. So the transport manager and I have agreed how we will treat them before the rest of the fleet catches up. Each lorry's software version is now recorded in the asset register next to its servicing history. The fleet portal is checked every week, and its notices come to the transport office and to my service desk. Where the manufacturer lets us choose, updates install on Saturday nights, when most of the fleet is parked. Any update that changes what a driver sees or does is briefed to drivers before it installs, in the same way as a change to our handheld software. When software reaches the things that move your goods, change management has to reach them as well, and someone has to decide whose job that is before the first update arrives. – Serguey Shinder

articles.title: How to Answer a Question You Don't Know on a Sales Call: Sales Tips and Sales Scripts for Founders and Engineers
articles.description: Every founder, solutions engineer and new AE eventually hits the moment: the buyer asks something you can't answer, and your brain goes blank. These sales tips and sales scripts show you how to handle "I don't know" on a sales call without losing credibility, and how to practise it until it feels normal. Done well, a question you can't answer can actually build sales confidence on both sides of the table. Why "I don't know" feels so dangerous If you come from engineering, you're trained to be right. In a code review, guessing is a bad habit. On a sales call, the instinct flips into panic: "If I don't know this, they'll think the product isn't real." So people do one of three things: Bluff. "Yes, we support that." (You're not sure.) This is the one that comes back to hurt you in procurement or onboarding. Ramble. Five minutes of thinking out loud until the original question is lost. Collapse. "Uh, I'm not sure, sorry," followed by a visible drop in energy for the rest of the call. Buyers don't expect you to know everything. They do watch how you behave when you don't. Calm and specific reads as trustworthy. Bluffing reads as risk. The 4-step answer: Acknowledge, Clarify, Commit, Continue Use this simple sales framework whenever you hit a question you can't answer. 1. Acknowledge honestly Say it plainly, once, without apologising three times. "Good question. I don't want to guess on that one." That sentence does more for your credibility than a confident wrong answer. 2. Clarify what they actually need Half the time, the question behind the question is easier than the question itself. Ask one of these discovery questions: "Can I ask what's driving that? Is it something you need on day one, or more of a future concern?" "When you say 'integrates with your CRM,' do you mean syncing contacts, logging calls, or something else?" "Is this a must-have for the decision, or a nice-to-know?" You'll often discover you can answer the real need, or that it's not a blocker at all. 3. Commit to a specific follow-up Vague promises ("I'll look into it") sound like brush-offs. Be specific about who, what and when. "I'll check with our CTO and send you a written answer by Thursday. Who else should be on that email?" Then write it down where they can see you doing it. On video calls, saying "I'm noting that now" is enough. 4. Continue the call Don't let one unknown hijack the conversation. Bridge back to what you were doing: "So I've got that one on my list. Going back to what you said about onboarding new reps, how long does that take today?" Sales scripts for the most common situations The technical deep-dive you can't go into "That's deeper than I can answer accurately right now. I'd rather get you the exact answer than a rough one. Would it help to set up 20 minutes with our engineer next week, or is a written answer enough?" The feature you don't have Don't pretend. Don't over-apologise either. "We don't do that today. Can you walk me through how you'd use it? I want to understand whether it's a blocker or whether there's another way to get you the same result." Pricing or contract terms you're unsure about "I don't want to quote you something I'd have to walk back. Let me confirm the exact terms and send them over tomorrow. In the meantime, is there a budget range you're working within?" Security and compliance questions This is where bluffing is most expensive. "Security questions deserve a precise answer. If you send me your questionnaire, I'll make sure it's filled in properly rather than me paraphrasing on a call." The question that's really an objection in disguise "Do you have customers in our industry?" sometimes means "I'm worried you won't understand us." Answer honestly, then address the worry: "Not yet in your industry specifically. What would you need to see to feel confident we understand how your team sells?" What not to do Don't guess and hope. A wrong "yes" on a call becomes a broken promise in writing. Don't say "great question" to everything. Once is fine. Every time sounds like a stalling tactic. Don't hand over control. "I don't know, what do you think?" without structure makes you sound lost, not curious. Don't forget the follow-up. The answer you promised is now part of your sales pitch. Missing it costs more than not knowing. A quick pre-call checklist Before any important sales call, spend five minutes on this: [ ] List the three questions you'd least like to be asked. [ ] For each one, decide: can I answer it, or do I need a "clarify and commit" script? [ ] Know who on your team can answer technical, pricing and security questions, and how fast. [ ] Have one bridge sentence ready to bring the call back on track. [ ] Decide in advance what you will never promise on a call (custom features, discounts, timelines). How to practise it Reading the 4 steps is easy. Doing them while a buyer is waiting for an answer is not. That moment of blank-mind panic is a reflex, and reflexes change with sales practice, not with notes. A simple drill for founders and teams: Ask a colleague to play the buyer and fire five hard questions at you, at least two of which you genuinely can't answer. Run the 4 steps out loud for each one. No pausing to think about the framework. Record it. Listen for apologies, rambling, and whether you actually got back to the call. Swap roles. Playing the buyer teaches you how calm "I don't know" sounds from the other side. Repeat it a few times and the first sentence ("I don't want to guess on that one") becomes automatic. That's the point: when the panic arrives, your mouth already knows what to do. Key takeaways Buyers judge how you handle not knowing more than the gap itself. Acknowledge, clarify, commit, continue. Use discovery questions to find the real need behind a hard question. Never bluff on features, pricing or security. Rehearse with sales role play until the response is a habit. If you want a place to practise hard questions like these against virtual customers who push back, that's what we're building at Kulissa.

articles.title: 40-image mood boards get 'let us think.' 3+3+1 sentence locks form direction
articles.description: Most mood boards fail on quantity. Forty pictures pasted into a collage show the client forty possible directions, and the only honest answer to that is "nice, let's look some more". A board that actually settles the direction has three parts on one page, and if any one of them is missing the page turns into wallpaper. The first part is three anchor images, each paired with a word. Three is a constraint that forces a decision: if the three do not point the same way, the direction is not thought through yet, and the board is simply hiding that. The word matters more than the image, because words are what people remember and repeat. It also has to be specific enough to be rejected. "Premium" is not a word in this sense - nobody can argue against it, so it excludes nothing. "Like a laboratory instrument" is a word: it rules out rounded consumer-electronics language, it can be checked against a sketch, and two people will disagree about it, which is exactly when a direction gets clarified. The second part is three counter-examples. Positive references say "go this way"; negative references say "do not go that way", and the negative ones carry more weight in a review, because they eliminate wrong answers directly. When somebody looks at a proposal and says it resembles one of the counter-examples, the judgement takes one sentence. Choose them carefully: do not pick ugly products, pick the ones that look good but are not what you want, because those are the only ones with discriminating power. Three successful competitors are usually the best pick, since the client has probably praised them somewhere else and needs the record cleared. The third part is the sentence, and it is the real deliverable. The client goes back and briefs their own boss; they will not remember your pictures, but they can remember twenty characters. "Like an instrument, not an appliance" can be compared against a drawing and drawn out. "Precise, restrained, professional" cannot - it is a pile of adjectives, and every listener reconstructs a different product from it. Read the sentence aloud once; if it does not roll, it will not survive the second hand-off, and the direction drifts at exactly that point. Two practical limits. Put 2 or 3 real material samples or close-up shots on the page so that "how it feels in the hand" is not argued in the abstract, but keep the whole page at 8 to 10 items; more than that and the attention scatters. If your content does not fit, you are trying to set more than one direction, and it should be two sessions. One page, one direction.

articles.title: Your AI Tools Are Getting Smarter. Why Does Your Work Still Feel So Fragmented?
articles.description: Switching models is easy. Keeping your decisions, project context, and next steps connected is the harder problem. You ask one AI to research an idea, another to challenge it, and a third to help you write. Then you become the courier. You copy the brief. Explain the decisions. Remind each tool what you already ruled out. Somewhere along the way, you lose the version you liked and start searching through old conversations. The answers might be useful. The process still needs work. I know this frustration because it’s part of why we started building 9xchat at the end of 2024. Disclosure: I’m a co-founder of 123sudo, the team behind 9xchat. This is both a workflow problem I care about and a product I help build. Back then, I could feel my work becoming tied to one AI app. My chats were there. My project context was there. The background I had spent time explaining was there. Trying another model was possible. Taking that accumulated understanding with me was harder. That made me question what I actually needed from AI. Was it another place to ask questions, or a better system for continuing the work? The work between the answers A quick question doesn’t need much continuity. A project does. When you’re building something over days or weeks, each conversation sits inside a larger story. There’s an audience you chose, an approach you rejected, a deadline you’re working toward, and a reason the latest draft looks the way it does. An individual answer can be excellent and still miss that story. You ask for a launch plan, and it recommends a channel you’ve already ruled out. You ask for a revision, and it changes something you deliberately kept. You start a new conversation and spend the opening messages rebuilding the brief. None of these moments looks dramatic on its own. Together, they make working with AI feel strangely repetitive. You’re not just doing the project. You’re maintaining the explanation of the project. That is the work between the answers. A better model is not automatically a better workflow Model capability matters. Different tasks benefit from different strengths, and choosing the right model can make a real difference. But model quality and workflow quality are not the same thing. A more capable model still needs relevant information. If it doesn’t have your current constraints or the reasons behind your decisions, you may get a polished answer that takes the project in the wrong direction. The question isn’t only: Which model should I use? It’s also: What does this model need to know so we can continue instead of starting again? That second question gets less attention, but it has become central to how I work. I don’t want every conversation to begin with a longer prompt. I want a reliable way to carry forward what matters, inspect it, and change it when the project changes. Before adding another tool, trace one task If your AI setup feels fragmented, start by looking at one real task. Choose something you recently completed: a proposal, an article, a research brief, a feature plan. Follow it from the first question to the finished result. Where did you repeat yourself? Look for the background information you explained more than once. Was it the audience? The tone? A technical constraint? A decision you thought was already settled? Repeated explanations show you which context needs a more deliberate home. What did you move between tools? Not every copy and paste is a problem. Sometimes a specialist tool is worth the handoff. But notice when you’re moving information simply because the next tool has no other way to access it. That’s coordination work. It deserves to be counted as part of the cost of your setup. Which decisions disappeared? Finding an old answer isn’t always enough. You also need to know whether it still applies. What did you choose? Why? What changed afterward? A saved transcript contains the conversation. It doesn’t necessarily give you a clear record of the current decision. What did each tool contribute? Some tools earn their place through a capability you genuinely need. Others remain in your workflow because you’ve become used to working around them. The point isn’t to force everything into one app. It’s to make sure the handoffs are helping you, rather than quietly becoming another job. ** Keep the useful context, not everything** My goal isn’t to make an AI remember every sentence I’ve ever written. It’s to make the right information available when it matters. For an ongoing project, I’d start with four things. The brief: What are we making, who is it for, and what should it accomplish? The constraints: What limits the work? Budget, tone, technical requirements, deadlines, or approaches we’ve ruled out. The decisions: What have we chosen, and why? The next action: Where did we stop, and what needs to happen next? Here’s a simple example: Project: An article for independent builders using multiple AI tools. Goal: Help readers identify where their workflow loses context. -Constraints: Practical rather than speculative. No invented productivity claims. Decision: Lead with the reader’s frustration, not the product’s features. Next action: Review the draft for unsupported claims and unnecessary promotion. That’s a small amount of information, but it gives the next conversation somewhere useful to begin. You can keep a project record like this in a document or a note. You don’t have to change tools to start working more deliberately. The system matters before the software does. Why we started building 9xchat At the end of 2024, the problem felt clear to me: I was investing time in conversations, but too much of their value felt tied to the app where they happened. I didn’t want choosing a different model to mean rebuilding my working context. That frustration helped push us to build 9xchat. Since then, it has evolved into an agentic workspace with multiple models, memory, notes, tools, Skills, and MCP connections. But the most meaningful change for me isn’t the growing feature list. It’s how much I now build with it. I use 9xchat every day, and I find it hard to imagine my working routine without it. Not because it does everything for me, but because it has become part of how I develop ideas and move work forward. That experience has made something very clear to me: The model matters. The system you build around it matters, too. What the system adds** In 9xchat, I can switch models within a conversation rather than treating each model as a completely separate working environment. Memory gives relevant information a way to persist beyond a single exchange. Notes provide a place for material I want to keep deliberately. Agents and reusable prompts help define recurring ways of working. These are different jobs. A note isn’t the same as a memory, and neither replaces checking the current brief. The distinction becomes even more important as the workspace gains more capabilities. The public documentation separates three building blocks: Tools let the assistant perform specific actions, such as searching the web or working with notes. Skills provide instructions for how it should approach a task or structure an answer. MCP connections make external tool collections available to the assistant. Tools, Skills, and MCP use in chat are part of Pro. To me, their value isn’t simply that the AI can do more things. It’s that they can support a more coherent way of working: relevant context, an appropriate method, and access to the tools needed for the task. That still requires judgment. A connected tool isn’t automatically the right tool. Saved information isn’t automatically current. A successful action isn’t proof that the entire task is correct. Being able to inspect and question the work remains essential. Using it is part of building it** At 123sudo, there’s always something to build or improve. Using 9xchat daily keeps showing me where the next improvement should be. Where did I have to repeat myself? What took too many steps? What did I expect the workspace to understand that it didn’t? Those moments are useful feedback precisely because they interrupt real work. I’m not only looking at the product from the outside. I’m inside it, trying to get something done, noticing what helps and what gets in the way. That doesn’t make my experience representative of everyone’s. We now have more than 1,000 users, bringing different projects, habits, and expectations. Their feedback matters alongside our own. People are also paying for access through monthly and lifetime licenses. That adds responsibility. A workspace has to earn its place through use, not just through a convincing demo. For clarity, Pro access and AI usage are separate: the current pricing offers monthly, yearly, and lifetime Pro options, while 9xchat AI credits are purchased separately. The ambition is bigger than the current product** One day, I’d love for 9xchat to help manage and coordinate far more of the systems we use at 123sudo. But that is a direction we want to explore, not a claim that it can run everything today. Broader capabilities need careful development: clear permissions, dependable behavior, ways to verify actions, and boundaries around what should require a person’s approval. Skills and MCP support are already here. What we build on top of them still needs to evolve through testing, feedback, and real use. I’m excited about that future. I’m also interested in the smaller improvements that make tomorrow’s work less frustrating than today’s. Sometimes that means another capability. Sometimes it means making an existing workflow clearer, more reliable, or easier to control. The milestone I’m proudest of** 9xchat is the first digital app I’ve helped build that I use every single day. Not just to test it. To do my own work. There’s something meaningful about helping build a tool and then repeatedly choosing it when you have something real to finish. I still see the rough edges. I still have ideas for what it should do better. In a way, that’s the point: using it keeps me close to the problem we started with. I wanted my work with AI to feel less scattered. I wanted to spend less effort carrying context and more effort building on it. That remains the goal. The next leap might be a more connected way of working A more capable model can open up new possibilities. I’m not dismissing that. But I no longer expect a model upgrade alone to fix a fragmented working process. If your brief is scattered, your decisions are buried, and every new conversation requires another introduction, the system around the model deserves attention too. Start with one project. Keep its brief current. Record the decisions that matter. Make the next action clear. Then judge your setup by a practical question: When you return to the work, can you continue, or do you have to explain it all again? Try keeping one project’s context connected in 9xchat.

articles.title: Our Network Supplier's Mistake Stopped Every Branch for a Day and Its Contract Capped What It Owed Us at Three Months of Fees
articles.description: A managed service provider runs our branch network, including the routers and firewalls at all thirty eight branches. In February 2025 one of its engineers applied a firewall change at six in the morning that blocked every branch from reaching our trading system. It was found and reversed shortly after two in the afternoon. For eight hours our counters took orders on paper, and some customers went elsewhere. Finance estimated the lost margin, overtime and credit notes at a little over two hundred thousand pounds. At the next board meeting our chief executive asked how much of that we would recover. I had to find out, and the answer was in a clause I had never read properly. The provider's total liability for any claim in a year was capped at the charges we had paid it in the previous three months, about thirty six thousand pounds. Loss of profit, revenue and business were excluded altogether, and those made up almost all of our loss. For failures to meet the service levels, the service credits were stated to be our sole remedy, and that day earned us about four thousand pounds. Our lawyers advised that a claim for negligence would meet the same cap. I had negotiated that contract in 2021 with our procurement team. I read the service level schedule line by line and left the liability clause to our lawyers, who reviewed it as a standard term, which it was. Nobody had asked them to compare it with what an outage would cost us, because nobody had worked that out. The board had assumed that outsourcing the network had moved the risk of it failing to someone else. Most of it had stayed with us. Every contract for a service whose failure can stop us trading now comes to the board with a one page summary prepared with finance. It states what a day without the service would cost us, what the supplier would pay in that case, and the gap we would carry. That gap is then either covered, negotiated down or accepted by name. At its renewal this year, our network contract's cap rose to twelve months of fees, and changes to branch firewalls now need our approval before they are applied. Outsourcing a service does not outsource the loss when it fails. The liability clause tells you how much of that loss you are still carrying, so read it with your finance director as well as your lawyer. – Serguey Shinder

articles.title: Music Customer Tag Management System Architecture & Design
articles.description: Music Customer Tag Management System Architecture & Design ——For Music Streaming Applications (Deliverable Solution) Background & Business Pain Points Music streaming apps accumulate massive user behavior data: song playback, search, collection, playlist creation, sharing, subscription payment, in-app interaction, etc. Most platforms face the following common problems: 1. Identity fragmentation: Users log in across mobile APP, in-car audio, smart speakers, WeChat mini-programs; anonymous users convert to registered users, leading to scattered user profiles. 2. Unstandardized tags: Different teams (recommendation, operation, membership) define tags independently, causing inconsistent metrics (e.g., "active user" has multiple definitions). 3. Imbalance between real-time & offline computing: Pure offline tags cannot support real-time recommendation & instant marketing; pure real-time tags lack global accuracy for large-scale crowd segmentation. 4. Weak tag governance: No version management, data lineage tracing, lifecycle expiration or access permission control, leading to redundant tags and data compliance risks. 5. Difficult business integration: Tags cannot be directly invoked by recommendation engines, push systems, marketing tools, resulting in low business value conversion. This solution designs a closed-loop tag management system to solve the above pain points. Core Architecture Philosophy 2.1 Unified Music Identity (MID) Construct a globally unique Music ID (MID) as the master user identifier. Map device ID, mobile number, third-party OAuth ID (WeChat/Apple/Google), anonymous session ID to one MID. Support anonymous user → registered user identity merging Link user behavior across all terminals (mobile, car, smart device, PC) MID serves as the only association key for all tag data 2.2 Full-Cycle Tag Metadata Governance Every tag must be pre-defined with complete metadata before going online: Metadata Item Description Example Tag ID & Name Unique identifier & readable name tag_001_music_taste_pop Business Purpose Which business scenario it serves Personalized recommendation / Membership churn intervention Tag Category Factual / Statistical / Rule-based / Model Statistical tag Calculation Logic SQL / Flink rule / ML model inference logic Count play times of pop songs in last 30 days Update Mode Offline full / Real-time incremental / Hybrid Hybrid Update Frequency Daily / Hourly / Second-level Daily offline + real-time incremental Data Owner Team responsible for the tag Recommendation Algorithm Team Effective & Expiration Time Tag lifecycle Valid from 2026-11-01 to 2027-11-01 Retention Period How long historical snapshots are kept 180 days Data Lineage Source tables & upstream dependencies User play log table ods_user_play_log Permission Level Public / Internal / Sensitive (PII) Sensitive (requires approval) 2.3 Hybrid Computing Model: Offline Full Recomputation + Real-time Incremental Update Offline pipeline: Generates stable baseline tags via batch computing. It is the source of truth for tag data. Used for large-scale audience segmentation, tag quality verification, historical trend analysis, and ML model training. Real-time pipeline: Processes user behavior events with low latency, updates lightweight tags incrementally, and overwrites the offline baseline for online query. Reconciliation mechanism: Periodically compare offline baseline and real-time incremental tag values, repair inconsistent data automatically. Tag versioning: Each tag calculation generates a version number; downstream services can specify a tag version to ensure result reproducibility. 2.4 Four-Dimensional Tag Classification (Mapped to Music Business) Tag Type Definition Music App Typical Examples Computing Mode Factual Tags Objective attributes directly collected from source data, no complex calculation Gender, age, city, registration channel, device model, membership level (free/paid/VIP), subscription expiry date, registration time Real-time / Near real-time Statistical Tags Aggregated metrics derived from user behavior over a sliding time window 30-day play count, average daily listening duration, top 3 favorite genres, favorite artists, playlist creation times, search frequency, weekly new song playback ratio Offline daily + real-time incremental Rule-based Tags Tags defined by explicit business rules combining multiple conditions High-value potential user (VIP expired within 30 days + 30-day play >100 times + no re-purchase), Churn-risk user (no login in 7 days + listening duration dropped by 50%), Night owl listener (play peak 23:00–02:00), Indie music enthusiast Offline full / Real-time rule engine Model Tags Tags generated by machine learning models Music taste embedding vector, churn probability score, price sensitivity level, genre preference score, ad tolerance level, potential paid conversion probability Offline batch inference / Online model serving Layered System Architecture The system adopts a five-layer architecture, from bottom to top: Layer 1: Data Source Layer Collect raw data from all touchpoints of the music app: User behavior logs: Play, pause, skip, search, collect, download, share, comment, playlist create/delete, radio tune-in User profile data: Registration info, bound phone, profile settings, minor mode status Transaction data: Subscription order, in-app purchase, coupon usage, refund records Content metadata: Song, artist, album, genre, language, release year, tag of songs Context data: Login time, geo location (optional, privacy-compliant), device type, network type, in-car / smart speaker terminal mark Data is collected via SDK, server logs, and binlog, then sent to Kafka as the unified data bus. Layer 2: Data Integration & Identity Resolution Layer Data Cleaning: Deduplication, invalid data filtering, format normalization MID Mapping Service: Map device ID / anonymous ID / third-party ID to unified MID; handle ID merging when anonymous users register Data Standardization: Unify behavior event formats, align dimension data (song ID → genre / artist) Layer 3: Tag Computing Layer Offline Computing Engine: Spark / Hive, executes full tag recalculation on a daily/weekly schedule Real-time Computing Engine: Flink, consumes Kafka behavior events, updates tags in near real-time Rule Engine: Executes rule-based tag logic, supports dynamic rule configuration without code release ML Model Service: Loads trained music taste / churn prediction models, executes batch & online inference Tag Version Controller: Manages tag version generation, snapshot creation, version rollback Data Quality Checker: Verifies tag coverage, null rate, outlier detection before tag release Layer 4: Tag Storage & Index Layer Storage Component Stored Content Purpose HBase / ClickHouse Detailed tag values for each MID (latest version + historical versions) Online point query & batch query Elasticsearch Inverted index of tag values Fast audience segmentation (filter users by tag conditions) MySQL / PostgreSQL Tag metadata, tag version info, data lineage, permission config Management console query HDFS Tag snapshots, historical backup, audit logs Disaster recovery & compliance audit Redis Hot user tag cache Low-latency real-time query (P99 < 20ms) Layer 5: Service & Application Layer Tag Query API: get_user_tags (single user), batch_get_user_tags (batch users), get_tag_metadata Audience Segmentation Engine: Visual rule builder, supports AND/OR/NOT conditions, segment estimation, segment export, scheduled refresh Tag Management Console: Web UI for tag creation, editing, version management, lifecycle configuration, data quality monitoring, usage statistics Permission & Audit Service: RBAC access control, sensitive tag approval flow, full operation audit log Data Export Service: Export audience ID lists to recommendation engine, push notification system, CRM, marketing platform End-to-End Data Pipeline Design 4.1 Offline Full Recomputation Pipeline (Daily Baseline) 1. Extract raw data from data warehouse (user logs, order data, content metadata) 2. Execute MID identity resolution to unify user IDs 3. Run Spark jobs to calculate statistical / rule-based / model tags 4. Data quality check: coverage rate > 95%, null value rate < 1%, outlier filtering 5. Write tag results to HBase & Elasticsearch, generate daily snapshot to HDFS 6. Tag version is marked as baseline, open to downstream services 4.2 Real-time Incremental Update Pipeline (Low Latency) 1. User behavior events (play, collect, subscribe) are sent to Kafka in real time 2. Flink job consumes events, updates incremental tag values (e.g., real-time play count, latest favorite genre) 3. Write updated tags to Redis (hot cache) and HBase 4. Overlay incremental results on the offline baseline for online query 5. Send change events to notify downstream recommendation & push systems 4.3 Hybrid Synchronization & Reconciliation Every 1 hour, run reconciliation tasks to compare offline baseline tags and real-time incremental tags If inconsistency exceeds threshold, trigger automatic repair (use offline baseline as priority) Keep full trace of tag change history for audit Business Scenario Implementation Details Scenario 1: Personalized Music Recommendation Required tags: Statistical tags (top genres, favorite artists), Model tags (music taste vector) Workflow: Recommendation engine calls get_user_tags API to fetch user tags → Generate daily recommendation playlist, radio station tuning, "similar to your favorites" list → User behavior feeds back to real-time pipeline, updates tags instantly → Recommendation results adjust dynamically Value: Improve recommendation CTR, increase user listening duration Scenario 2: Precision Marketing & Campaign Operations Required tags: Factual tags (city, device), Rule-based tags (high-value potential, churn-risk), Statistical tags (activity level) Workflow: Operators use console to build audience segment (e.g., pop music lover + free user + 30-day play >60min) → Segment engine filters MID list → Push system sends targeted in-app message / coupon → Tag system tracks campaign exposure & conversion, evaluates tag effectiveness Value: Improve marketing conversion rate, reduce invalid push annoyance Scenario 3: Membership Lifecycle Management Required tags: Factual tags (VIP level, expiry date), Model tags (churn probability), Rule-based tags (renewal-intent user) Workflow: Identify users with high churn probability via model tags → Trigger real-time intervention (discount coupon, exclusive playlist) → Track whether user renews subscription → Feed renewal result back to model for retraining Value: Increase VIP renewal rate, reduce membership churn Scenario 4: Content Curation & Music Supply Required tags: Statistical tags (genre preference distribution), Model tags (music taste cluster) Workflow: Content team queries audience segments (e.g., indie music enthusiasts) → Analyze segment size, listening habits → Create exclusive playlists / promote emerging artists → Recommendation engine pushes content to target segments → Measure playlist adoption rate via tag system Value: Optimize content supply, improve long-tail music exposure Scenario 5: Risk Control & Compliance Required tags: Factual tags (minor status, device), Rule-based tags (abnormal playback behavior) Workflow: Detect abnormal behaviors (e.g., batch skipping, machine playback) via rule tags → Trigger risk control interception → Minor protection mode automatically enabled based on age tag → Support user data deletion request (cascade delete all tags under MID for GDPR/CCPA compliance) Value: Reduce fraudulent traffic, meet data privacy regulations Permission, Security & Compliance Design 6.1 RBAC Permission Model Role Permission Scope Tag Administrator Create/edit/delete tags, manage metadata, configure lifecycle, assign permissions Tag Developer Develop tag calculation logic, debug pipelines, view data lineage Operations User Use tags for audience segmentation, export audience lists, view tag values (non-sensitive only) Auditor Read-only access to all tags, view audit logs, export compliance reports 6.2 Data Security Encryption: TLS for data in transit; AES-256 for data at rest; field-level encryption for PII tags (age, phone, location) Sensitive Tag Control: Access to sensitive tags requires secondary approval; access records are saved in audit log Anonymization: For non-essential scenarios, use anonymized MID instead of raw user identifiers 6.3 Compliance (GDPR / CCPA / Local PIPL) Support right to be forgotten: When user requests account deletion, cascade delete all tag data and historical snapshots of the corresponding MID Tag retention period is enforced automatically; expired tags are purged without manual intervention Full audit log records all tag query, modification, export, deletion operations (operator, timestamp, target MID scope) Capacity Planning & Disaster Recovery Storage Capacity: Estimated based on total MID count × average tag count per user × historical snapshot retention days; needs stress test verification Computing Resource: Offline Spark cluster resources are allocated according to daily tag recalculation data volume; Flink real-time cluster is scaled based on Kafka event QPS Performance Baseline: Single-user tag query P99 latency, batch query throughput, audience segmentation response time — all need to be verified via stress testing Disaster Recovery: ¡Offline tag baseline: RPO < 24 hours, RTO < 4 hours (batch job rerun) ¡Real-time tag service: Multi-replica deployment, automatic failover, RTO < 30 seconds ¡Regular snapshot backup to HDFS for disaster recovery Phased Implementation Roadmap Phase Business Integration Month 3–4 Real-time incremental pipeline, rule-based tag engine, audience segmentation service, integration with recommendation & push systems Phase 3: Intelligence & Governance fragmentation, tag inconsistency and computing timeliness for music streaming apps. By combining Unified MID, full tag governance, hybrid offline & real-time computing, and scenario-driven tag classification, it provides a reliable, scalable and compliant foundation for personalized recommendation, precision operation, membership management, content curation and risk control. The return URL is not a payment confirmation
articles.description: A checkout we reviewed marked orders as paid when the customer landed on /return?status=success after 3DS. It looked fine in testing, because the redirect and the gateway result always agreed. In production they drifted apart in three ways: The customer pressed Back during the challenge and later reopened the return URL from browser history. The order flipped to paid on a stale redirect. The bank's ACS confirmed the challenge, but the authorization then declined at the issuer. The redirect still said the 3DS step succeeded, so the order was marked paid while no money moved. Anyone could edit the query string. Changing status=failed to status=success worked on a test order, because the handler never checked a signature. The redirect only tells you the browser came back. It says nothing about the transaction. What we changed: the return page now shows "checking your payment" and never writes order state. State changes only from the signed webhook, or from a server-side status call by transaction id when the webhook is late. The page polls our own order status for up to about 20 seconds, then tells the customer we'll email them. The unpaid-but-shipped orders stopped, and so did the paid-but-not-fulfilled ones. Do you let the return URL touch order state at all, or is that strictly webhook territory in your system? Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

Setup The files are TypeScript and run on Node 22.6 or newer with type stripping (tested here on Node 24.7): node --experimental-strip-types run.ts Imports between files need the .ts extension, and types use import type, which this mode requires. For plain JavaScript, rename to .mjs, delete the annotations and the import type lines. The two endpoints The REST API is documented on the developers page and, for pumpfun specifically, on the pumpfun API page. Everything is a GET that returns JSON, with no key. The public limit is about 20 calls a minute and answers are cached for up to a minute, so there is no point in polling faster than that. GET https://copy.top/v1/traders?platform=pumpfun&window=30d&sort=realized&limit=10 returns a leaderboard. window is the period, sort=realized ranks by realized profit, limit is the number of rows. GET https://copy.top/v1/coins/hot?window=1h returns coins that tracked traders bought in the last hour, with counts and dollar totals. I checked the field names below against real responses. A trader row has handle, name, pnl, realized, unrealized, roi, winRate (a number from 0 to 1), closed (closed positions), followers, copiers and a few more. A coin row has symbol, token (the address), traders, topTraders, topStillIn, sold, boughtUsd, soldUsd, firstBuyMinAgo, lastBuyMinAgo and buyers. A handle that starts with pf_ is a pumpfun account. Types Only the fields the script reads. export interface Trader { handle: string; name: string; pnl: number; realized: number; unrealized: number; roi: number; winRate: number; // 0 to 1 closed: number; // closed positions in the window followers: number; copiers: number; url: string; } export interface Leaderboard { window: string; sort: string; traders: Trader[]; export interface HotCoin { chain: string; token: string; // address symbol: string; mcap: number | null; traders: number; // tracked traders who bought it in the window topTraders: number; // how many of them are top traders topStillIn: number; // top traders still holding sold: number; boughtUsd: number; soldUsd: number; firstBuyMinAgo: number; lastBuyMinAgo: number; buyers: string[]; export interface HotCoins { at: string; coins: HotCoin[]; Step 1: a small fetch wrapper The wrapper does three things: it builds the query string, it stops a hung request after 20 seconds with AbortSignal.timeout, and it throws on a non-200 answer. The second function waits 1.5 seconds before it calls, which keeps a run far below the public limit. import type { Leaderboard, HotCoins } from "./types.ts"; // polite: the public limit is about 20 calls a minute async function get<T>(path: string, params: Record<string, string | number>): Promise<T> { return (await res.json()) as T; export async function getLeaderboard(limit = 10): Promise<Leaderboard> { return get<Leaderboard>("/traders", { platform: "pumpfun", window: "30d", sort: "realized", limit, }); export async function getHotCoins(): Promise<HotCoins> { await sleep(DELAY_MS); return get<HotCoins>("/coins/hot", { window: "1h" }); A run makes exactly two requests. Step 2: the runner With no argument the script calls the live API. With --fixture it reads fixture.json instead and makes no network call. With --save it also writes the live answers to fixture.json. The second table filters the coins with traders >= 3, so only coins where several tracked traders bought in the last hour remain. Some coins have a blank or invisible symbol, so label falls back to the first characters of the address. import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs"; import { getLeaderboard, getHotCoins } from "./api.ts"; let board: Leaderboard; let hot: HotCoins; else { board = await getLeaderboard(10); hot = await getHotCoins(); /[A-Za-z0-9]/.test(c.symbol) ? c.symbol : c.token.slice(0, 6); Live use is node --experimental-strip-types run.ts.
