articles.title: How AIClaw 3.12.14 Shows Sub-Agent Progress Without Leaving the Parent Chat
articles.description: A parent agent can delegate a review and keep working while the child runs. From the parent chat, it is useful to see whether the review is still running and what the child has recorded, especially when several tasks are underway. AIClaw v3.12.14 adds a read-only sub-agent view to the desktop conversation details panel. Release notes Follow the task tree from the parent chat On a desktop viewport at least 1,280 CSS pixels wide, open Conversation Details in an existing chat. If that chat has delegated sessions, the panel lists them by task title and status. A child that delegates work of its own appears with another level of indentation. The renderer builds this tree from session parent IDs. Two sessions in the same workspace can have different task trees. Desktop layout · Sub-agent panel Selecting a child opens its transcript inside the panel. The renderer requests that child's saved history and combines it with live timeline entries by entry ID, giving the live copy precedence when an ID appears in both. A live turn can show a running or interrupted state while the parent chat stays open. When there is no live status, the panel can use the status supplied with the session summary. Panel implementation · Session summaries What the panel and tests cover The panel reads history and renders text and expandable steps. Opening it leaves the active conversation in place and does not resume the child. The Electron smoke fixture checks stored history, verifies that no child resume call occurs, and injects turn events to check running and interrupted states. A Go collaboration test separately checks that a completed child can be identified after returning an answer. These checks use fixtures. They cover the read-only interaction and status transitions, while the quality and timing of delegated work depend on the actual run. Electron smoke test · Go collaboration tests · Release workflow

articles.title: FastMRZ 3 - Passport MRZ Extraction in Pure Python, No Tesseract
articles.description: If you have ever built KYC onboarding, hotel check-in or border-control software, you know the MRZ: the two or three lines of <<<-padded text at the bottom of a passport, ID card or visa. Reading it sounds simple. It is 37 possible characters (A-Z, 0-9 and <) in a fixed layout defined by ICAO 9303. In practice, most Python MRZ tools come with the same setup ritual: Install Tesseract at system level Download a special MRZ traineddata file Copy it into the correct tessdata folder Make sure all of that also exists in your Docker image, Lambda layer, CI runner and the Windows laptop of whoever joins the team next And after all that, it still struggles with phone photos that are skewed, blurred or badly lit. The first versions of FastMRZ had the same problem, because they used Tesseract under the hood. With FastMRZ 3, I removed Tesseract completely. What's new in FastMRZ 3 No Tesseract. FastMRZ now ships its own ONNX text recogniser, trained only for the MRZ character set. Pure Python install. The only dependencies are numpy, opencv-python-headless and pymupdf. No system packages, no traineddata files. More accurate than the Tesseract-based versions, because the recogniser only has to tell apart 37 characters in one fixed font, not every glyph in every language. More input types. File paths, NumPy arrays, Base64 strings, raw bytes, PDFs and plain MRZ text. Batch processing in parallel. More document formats. TD1, TD2, TD3, MRV-A and MRV-B. Install pip install fastmrz That's the whole setup. Quick start from fastmrz import FastMRZ fast_mrz = FastMRZ() details = fast_mrz.get_details("passport.jpg") print(details) Output (trimmed): status is SUCCESS only when the format and every ICAO 9303 check digit are valid. Otherwise it is FAILURE, and status_message tells you the first problem found. If no MRZ is found in the image at all, you get: No exceptions to catch, no silent garbage. Either the data passed the checksums or you're told why it didn't. Every input type you'll actually use In real systems, images rarely arrive as files on disk. They come from an upload endpoint, a camera frame or a scanned PDF. FastMRZ takes all of them: # Raw MRZ text instead of parsed fields text = fast_mrz.get_details("passport.jpg", ignore_parse=True) # OpenCV / camera frame (BGR or grayscale ndarray) details = fast_mrz.get_details(image_array, input_type="numpy") # From a web or mobile client details = fast_mrz.get_details(b64_string, input_type="base64") # Straight from an upload or S3 object details = fast_mrz.get_details(image_bytes, input_type="bytes") # Scanned PDF - uses the first page with an MRZ details = fast_mrz.get_details("scan.pdf", input_type="pdf") # Already have the MRZ string? Parse and validate only details = fast_mrz.get_details(mrz_string, input_type="text") Two more helpers: # Check digits only result = fast_mrz.validate_mrz(mrz_string) # {"is_valid": ..., "status_message": ...} # Get the rectified MRZ crop, useful for audit logs or manual review strip = fast_mrz.get_mrz_image("passport.jpg") Batch processing results = fast_mrz.get_details_batch(["a.jpg", "b.jpg", "c.jpg"]) Results come back in input order Runs in parallel. workers defaults to your CPU count, capped at 8 Expect roughly 1.5x the throughput of a plain loop on a 4-core CPU A file that can't be read doesn't stop the batch. Its entry just comes back as FAILURE with a message It takes the same options as get_details: get_details_batch(inputs, input_type="imagepath", ignore_parse=False, include_checkdigit=True, workers=None) How it works Locate. OpenCV contour detection plus an ONNX model find the MRZ region, even when the document isn't perfectly aligned in the photo. Rectify. The MRZ strip is cropped, deskewed and normalised. Recognise. A small ONNX model reads the characters. Because it only has to handle the 37 MRZ symbols in the OCR-B font, it can be far smaller and more reliable on this job than a general-purpose OCR engine. Validate. Every check digit defined by ICAO 9303 is verified, and the fields are parsed into clean, structured output. Everything runs locally on CPU. No document image ever leaves your machine, which matters when you're handling passports. Supported documents Format Used on Lines x chars TD1 ID cards 3 x 30 TD2 Older ID cards, some visas 2 x 36 TD3 Passports 2 x 44 MRV-A Visas (large) MRV-B Visas (small) Migrating from PassportEye # PassportEye from passporteye import read_mrz mrz = read_mrz("passport.jpg") data = mrz.to_dict() # FastMRZ data = FastMRZ().get_details("passport.jpg") No Tesseract install, and the status field tells you whether the checksums passed. Upgrading from FastMRZ 1.x / 2.x Remove Tesseract from your Dockerfile and setup scripts. You no longer need it. If you still pass the old tesseract_path or tessdata_path arguments, FastMRZ 3 ignores them and raises a FutureWarning, so you can clean them up at your own pace. Where it fits KYC and customer onboarding in banking and fintech Hotel, airline and car-rental check-in Travel, immigration and visa processing Any back-office workflow where staff type passport details by hand today Try it, break it, tell me GitHub: https://github.com/sivakumar-mahalingam/fastmrz PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/fastmrz/ FastMRZ is open source under Apache-2.0. The most useful thing you can send me is a failure case. If FastMRZ can't read one of your documents, open an issue with a redacted sample and I'll use it to improve the model. And if it saves you a Tesseract install, a star on GitHub helps other developers find it.

articles.title: The Strategic Executive vs. the Tactical Executive
articles.description: In technology leadership, the difference between a tactical executive and a strategic executive is not simply a matter of style. It reflects two different ways of understanding problems, making decisions, and creating value for the organization. The tactical executive focuses primarily on immediate actions and technical details. When a security incident occurs, for example, this leader may concentrate on identifying the vulnerability, applying the patch, and restoring the system. This response can be necessary, especially during a crisis, because tactical execution provides speed, control, and short-term stability. However, the tactical executive often remains focused on the symptoms of a problem. The discussion may center on the specific bug, the system failure, or the operational task that needs to be completed. Although this approach can solve the immediate issue, it may not address the organizational or governance gap that allowed the problem to happen in the first place. The strategic executive, by contrast, looks beyond the immediate event. After a security incident, this leader does not spend most of the discussion explaining the technical details of the patch. Instead, the strategic executive asks what the incident revealed about the company’s processes, security practices, governance, and risk exposure. The focus shifts from “How did we fix the problem?” to “How can we prevent this type of problem from happening again?” This distinction can also be seen in communication with the board. A tactical technology executive may present engineering activities such as completed tasks, merged pull requests, or infrastructure changes. A strategic executive translates those activities into business outcomes. Instead of saying that the company needs to modernize its architecture, the strategic leader explains that the current system is delaying revenue-generating features, increasing costs, or limiting the company’s ability to compete. The tactical executive typically sees technology through the lens of capability and execution. The strategic executive sees it through the lens of risk, return, and competitive advantage. For the strategic leader, technology is not an end in itself. It is a means of increasing revenue, reducing costs, protecting the company, improving scalability, and creating a stronger position in the market. This strategic perspective offers several important advantages. First, it improves decision-making. When technical investments are connected to business priorities, the board and senior leadership can evaluate them more effectively. They can understand not only what a project costs, but also what value it may create and what risks it may reduce. Second, strategic leadership improves resource allocation. A strategic executive can show how engineering capacity is divided among innovation, growth, scale, and maintenance. This makes trade-offs visible. For example, dedicating more resources to security may temporarily reduce feature development, but it can also protect revenue, customer trust, and regulatory compliance. Third, strategic executives build greater trust. They do not hide behind technical language or present themselves as heroes who personally solve every problem. Instead, they describe the strengths and weaknesses of the engineering system. Successes are connected to scalable processes, while failures are treated as systemic gaps that the organization must address. Finally, strategic leadership gives technology a stronger role in the future of the company. A strategic executive can identify technical capabilities that may improve the organization’s competitive position over the next twelve to eighteen months. The focus is not on adopting technology because it is fashionable, but on understanding how it can accelerate growth, reduce the cost of scaling, or improve the company’s ability to innovate. Being tactical is not inherently negative. Tactical execution is essential for responding to incidents, delivering projects, and maintaining daily operations. The limitation arises when a leader remains exclusively tactical and never connects immediate actions to broader business consequences. The most effective technology executives are capable of operating tactically when necessary while thinking strategically at all times. They can understand the technical details, but they do not allow those details to dominate the conversation. Their responsibility is to transform complexity into clarity and technical activity into business value. In the end, the strategic executive is more than a manager of systems and teams. This leader becomes a partner in defining priorities, allocating capital, managing risk, and shaping the company’s future. That is why strategic thinking is one of the most important qualities a technology executive can develop.

articles.title: The Swap Is Only the Beginning: 5 Things That Happen Between Your Wallet and a TRON Transaction
articles.description: TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN. tronseven.com A practical look at wallet permissions, smart contracts, network resources, and what users should understand before exchanging TRON tokens. You select two tokens. You enter an amount. You connect your wallet. You press Swap. A few seconds later, the transaction appears on the blockchain. It sounds simple. And from a user's perspective, it should be. But underneath that clean interface is a sequence of technical operations that deserves more attention than it usually gets. A crypto swap is not just a conversion between two numbers. It is an interaction between a wallet, a smart contract, token permissions, network resources, and blockchain settlement. Understanding those moving parts can help users make better decisions, avoid unnecessary mistakes, and evaluate swap platforms more intelligently. Let's break it down using the TRON ecosystem as our example. Your wallet is more than a place to store tokens A common misconception is that connecting a wallet means handing control of your cryptocurrency to an application. These are two very different things. A wallet is the interface through which you manage your keys and authorize blockchain interactions. A non-custodial application should allow you to interact with smart contracts without taking possession of your assets. That distinction matters. Before using any swap service, ask yourself: Does the application require you to deposit funds into an account? Can you inspect the contract receiving your transaction? Does the wallet clearly display the action you are approving? Are you being asked to sign something unrelated to the swap? Never approve a wallet request simply because a website tells you to. Your private keys and recovery phrase should remain private. A legitimate swap interface should never need your seed phrase. Token approval and token exchange are not necessarily the same operation This is one of the most important concepts in smart-contract-based token exchanges. Many TRC-20 tokens implement an allowance mechanism. In simple terms, a token holder can authorize a particular smart contract to spend a specified amount of tokens on their behalf. This is commonly handled through an approval transaction. Why does this matter? Because approving a token allowance and executing a swap are conceptually different actions. An approval establishes permission. A swap executes an exchange according to the relevant contract logic. Users should understand what allowance they are granting, which contract receives it, and whether the requested amount is reasonable. This is particularly important when interacting with unfamiliar decentralized applications. A good habit is to review permissions rather than treating every wallet confirmation as an ordinary login. TRON network resources are part of the transaction experience TRON has a resource model that includes Bandwidth and Energy. These resources are used when transactions are processed on the network. Bandwidth relates primarily to transaction data, while Energy is associated with the computational work required to execute smart contracts. This creates an interesting difference between simply transferring a token and interacting with a more complex smart contract. For users, the practical question is straightforward: What will this transaction actually cost me? The answer can depend on available network resources, the contract operation, and the transaction's execution requirements. This is why looking only at the advertised exchange rate is not enough. A useful swap interface should make transaction costs understandable before the user confirms the operation. The displayed exchange rate is only one part of the decision Imagine exchanging USDT for another TRC-20 asset. You see a quote that looks attractive. Should you immediately confirm? Not necessarily. There are several things worth checking: Exchange rate: How much of the receiving asset is estimated for your input? Price impact: Could your trade size affect the execution price? Liquidity: Is there sufficient liquidity for the selected token pair? Network costs: What resources are required to execute the transaction? Minimum received: Is there protection against receiving substantially less than expected? These details help explain why two swap interfaces can present different experiences even when they support the same blockchain. A better approach is to compare the complete transaction rather than focusing on one attractive number. Blockchain transparency should be something users can actually verify One of the strongest properties of public blockchains is that transactions can be independently inspected. You do not have to rely entirely on a platform's marketing description. On TRON, TRONSCAN provides a way to investigate transactions, addresses, and smart-contract activity. This is an important part of evaluating any swap application. Look for: A publicly identifiable smart-contract address. Contract source code and verification information. Transaction records that can be inspected independently. Clear documentation explaining how the application works. An audit or security review can be useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee that a system is risk-free. Users should still examine the available information and understand the risks associated with smart-contract interactions. Where does TronSeven fit into this picture? These principles become much more interesting when applied to an actual TRON-native swap application. One project worth examining is TronSeven. Website: https://tronseven.com TronSeven presents itself as a non-custodial exchange focused on TRON assets, including TRX and TRC-20 tokens such as USDT and USDC. The platform lists wallet connectivity through: TronLink Trust Wallet WalletConnect It also provides publicly accessible smart-contract information and a TRONSCAN link, giving users a starting point for independently investigating its on-chain infrastructure. Another interesting aspect is its approach to network resources. The project describes using TRON Energy to cover swap-related network costs. Rather than evaluating a swap platform solely by its interface, users can examine these technical details and decide whether its approach fits their requirements. You can explore the application and its published information here: https://tronseven.com A simple checklist before your next TRON swap Before confirming an exchange, take a moment to review these points: Network: Are both assets on the correct blockchain? Token contract: Have you checked that you selected the intended token? Wallet: Is the application requesting only the permissions necessary for the operation? Allowance: Do you understand which contract is authorized to spend your tokens? Quote: Have you reviewed the expected receiving amount and price impact? Resources: Do you understand the potential network costs? Verification: Can you inspect the relevant contract and transaction information? This checklist takes less time than recovering from a transaction made without understanding what you approved. Final thoughts: Better swaps begin with better understanding The TRON ecosystem continues to offer practical opportunities for people using stablecoins, decentralized applications, and TRC-20 assets. But a good swap experience should involve more than a convenient button. It should combine understandable transaction details, clear wallet interactions, transparent smart-contract information, and a process users can independently investigate. That's the perspective worth bringing to every exchange. If you're exploring TRON-native token swaps, take a closer look at TronSeven, examine its available contract information, and see how its swap interface works. Explore TronSeven: https://tronseven.com

What WooCommerce Automation Really Costs (Build, Tools and AI)
articles.description: Store owners usually ask what the tool costs. The better question is what the whole project costs over a year. Here is how I break down automation around WooCommerce. Build cost by tier These are planning ranges based on typical freelance work, not fixed quotes. Tier What you get Range Starter One or two workflows, such as order alerts and a spreadsheet log $300 to $800 Standard Four to eight workflows, error alerts, retries, documentation $800 to $2,500 Advanced Custom APIs, AI features, CRM or accounting sync, approvals $2,500 to $8,000+ Cost follows hours, not tools. At roughly $40 to $90 an hour, a Starter build is 6 to 12 hours and a Standard build 15 to 40. What raises the hours is rarely the first connection. It is refunds, partial shipments, failed payments, missing data and retries after an outage. Zapier, Make or n8n All three can listen to WooCommerce events through webhooks and the REST API. They bill differently, which is where surprises come from. Zapier: fastest setup, free tier, paid plans from roughly $20 to $30 a month. Every step counts as a task, so long workflows get expensive. Make: free tier, entry plans around $10 a month. Counts operations per step. n8n: cloud plans from about $20 a month, or self-hosted on a small server for roughly $5 to $20 a month, plus the time to maintain and secure it. Prices change often, so check each pricing page. Before you commit, multiply the steps in a workflow by your monthly orders to see what the platform will really charge. Where AI fits AI helps when a workflow has to read text: support triage, drafting replies, product descriptions for review, summarising reviews. It is not needed for rules like "notify the manager above a certain order total", and plain rules are cheaper and more predictable. AI providers bill by usage. For a small or mid-sized store that is often a few dollars to tens of dollars a month, but it depends on volume, so set a monthly cap. Keep a person in the loop for prices, refunds and anything legal. Low-risk tasks like tagging can run on their own. Does it pay back? Say six hours a week of order entry, shipping emails and stock checks at $25 an hour. That is about $7,800 a year. A $1,200 build plus $40 a month in tools costs about $1,680 in year one, so the build is recovered in roughly eight to ten weeks. If the task takes thirty minutes a week, it will not pay back for a long time. Leave it alone. Risks to budget for Duplicate actions when a workflow runs twice Silent failures with no error alert API changes that need an occasional fix Customer data passing through every connected service Testing on the live store instead of a staging copy FAQ Do I need AI for store automation? No. Order alerts, stock warnings and tracking emails are rule-based and need no AI. Can automation break my store? A badly built workflow can send duplicate emails or miss orders, but it does not change the store itself. Build on a copy, test refunds and set error alerts. Who should own the workflows? You. They should live in your own platform accounts, with documentation. Large log records in Dynatrace: limits, native support and best practices
articles.description: A ticket lands: « the partner call is cut off halfway through in the logs ». You open the record and it simply stops. The payload crossed a limit somewhere. Large log records in Dynatrace raise exactly this operational question: how big can a record be, and on which path? This article starts from that decision (keep, split or shrink a record) and checks every figure against the official documentation, read on 12 November 2026. It applies to Dynatrace SaaS (Grail and OpenPipeline). I did not verify Dynatrace Managed limits for this piece, so I quote none. If cost is a new topic for you, read log costs: ingest, retain and query first. The typical case: a record of several hundred kilobytes A billing XML message, a partner API’s JSON response, a stack trace with its full context: such events quickly grow past a kilobyte. The vendor’s post puts this range between a few hundred kilobytes and several megabytes. For a long time the default answer was to truncate or split upstream, at the price of lost context. The same post announces native support for single log events of up to 10 MB, with no configuration, through OneAgent, OpenTelemetry, the API or other collectors. It is vendor presentation material: it does not say what happens above 10 MB. The reference documentation spells out the conditions. Large log records in Dynatrace: the limits to check The Log Management and Analytics default limits page gives these values: Log entry body (content): 10 MB, but only 512 kB for logs processed by the Classic pipeline. API request: 10 MB at the endpoint; a batch above 16 MB after preprocessing is rejected with HTTP 413. Records per request: 50,000. Attributes: 500 per log, attribute value capped at 32 kB, key at 100 bytes, 5 levels of nested objects. Size after processing in OpenPipeline: 16 MB, according to the OpenPipeline limits page. Keep the first line in mind: « 10 MB » is not a universal promise. The Classic path stays at 512 kB. If a long log vanishes or stops short, check which pipeline it goes through first. This capture is the real output of commands run on a test file. The 600,000-byte record exceeds the Classic limit but stays far below 10 MB. Send a big record and check its size Here is how to test on a pre-production environment. Create an API token with the log ingest scope and keep it in an environment variable. Build a JSON file with a large content field. Send it with curl to the ingest API and note the status code. Query the logs in DQL to measure the length of the content received. fetch logs | filter log.source == "payment-gateway" | fieldsAdd size = stringLength(content) | sort size desc | limit 10 A 204 means everything was accepted. The documentation also lists 400 or 200 depending on whether all or some events fall outside the accepted time range. If the measured size is below what you sent, a limit cut the content: go back to the list above. For syntax, see log pattern analysis. What to do with a huge log once ingested A multi-megabyte record costs storage, queries and reading time. Ask three questions in this order: Who reads it? If nobody reads the whole body, extract the useful fields (error code, order ID) and keep the rest for investigations. Which part is sensitive? A big JSON often hides personal data. See masking in OpenPipeline. Which pipeline fits? Route these logs to a dedicated pipeline with its own rules: create and route a pipeline. Watch two processing limits. An extracted attribute is truncated to 4,096 characters when added to the event template. Each DQL processor script is limited to 8,192 characters, according to the OpenPipeline limits page. Best practices Measure the real size of your biggest events before changing anything. Confirm the pipeline (Classic or OpenPipeline) of every source that produces big logs. Do not use logs to carry files: a log is an event, not storage. Extract useful fields at ingest and drop the rest when you can. Test a send above the limit in pre-production to learn the real behaviour: the documentation I read does not describe it for every path. Frequently asked questions What is the maximum log size in Dynatrace? According to the SaaS documentation, an entry body can reach 10 MB, but only 512 kB on the Classic pipeline. Check the limits page before committing, as it changes. Should I split large logs before sending them? Not necessarily on the 10 MB path, according to the vendor’s post. On the Classic pipeline the 512 kB limit still applies. Measure with the DQL query above. Does this apply to Dynatrace Managed? This article covers SaaS only. For Managed, read the Managed documentation and do not reuse these figures. Conclusion Large log records in Dynatrace pass up to 10 MB on the Grail path, but the Classic pipeline cuts at 512 kB: the incident at the top often comes down to that detail. Measure, route, extract. articles.title: ESP32-P4 boot loop (CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET): building a homelab watchdog in ESPHome
articles.description: My homelab's monitoring has a daft weak spot. Uptime Kuma runs on my NAS. So if the NAS goes down, the thing that's meant to tell me the NAS is down goes with it. I've got a script on another box that restarts Kuma if it dies, but that's still the homelab watching itself. So I bought a Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH. Wired Ethernet, can run off PoE, no WiFi at all. My first idea was to move Uptime Kuma onto it. That was never happening, it's a microcontroller, not a Linux box. So on 13 October 2026 I settled on something it can actually do: be a small, dumb, independent watchdog that doesn't rely on any of my servers to send an alert. What it does Every 60 seconds it checks 10 things: Uptime Kuma, SSH on the NAS, the reverse proxy, both Proxmox nodes, my agent box, Vaultwarden, the router's web page, AdGuard DNS, and the internet (1.1.1.1:443). Most of those are just a TCP connect. DNS is a proper one: it builds a real A-record query for cloudflare.com by hand and sends it straight at AdGuard, then checks the answer has the right ID, no error and at least one record. An open port doesn't mean DNS is working. 3 failures in a row and it posts 🔴 DOWN to Discord, straight from the board. The first good check after that posts 🟢 RECOVERED with how many minutes it was down. Three strikes stops one dropped packet waking me up. If it can't send (say the internet's gone), the alert goes in a queue. It keeps the newest 20 and retries every cycle. Every cycle it also pushes to an Uptime Kuma push monitor with a 120 second heartbeat. So Kuma watches the board while the board watches Kuma. If either dies, the other one says so. All the checks run in their own FreeRTOS task, so a target that hangs on connect never blocks the rest of the board. I wrote it as ESPHome YAML plus one C++ header. ESPHome gives me OTA updates, a web page and the Ethernet setup for free, and the header does the actual checking. Compile trap: socket() is ambiguous First compile failed on something stupid. ESPHome has its own esphome::socket namespace, so a bare socket() call inside my code was ambiguous. You have to use the global ones: ::socket, ::connect, ::close and so on. After that it compiled clean. RAM 13.5%, flash 695 KB. Tiny. The boot loop I flashed it from my Mac late on 13 October and it went straight into a boot loop. Reset every 3.2 seconds or so, no app log at all, just this: rst:0x10 (CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET) No app log means it's dying before my code even runs, so it wasn't my watchdog code. It was the build. I'd copied board: esp32-p4-evboard because that's what you'd reach for. Turns out in ESPHome that board means the engineering sample P4, the pre-production chips before revision 3. My board has a production chip, revision v3.2. So the firmware was built for the wrong silicon, and the chip's low-power watchdog reset it every few seconds. The fix was to stop naming a board at all and just tell ESPHome the chip: esp32: variant: esp32p4 engineering_sample: false cpu_frequency: 360MHZ # 400MHz on the P4 is marked experimental in ESPHome flash_size: 16MB framework: type: esp-idf That set the minimum chip revision to 3.1 in the build config, and it booted fine. If you've got a P4 board in a boot loop with CHIP_LP_WDT_RESET and no log, check you're not building for the engineering sample. The first live flash sent nothing anywhere On 15 October it went on the network for real. Kuma push: 404. Discord: 400. The OTA password was, word for word, REPLACE-with-a-long-random-string. Yeah. The first flash had used the example secrets file with the placeholders still in. Nothing was broken, it just had nothing real to talk to. I rebuilt with proper secrets and pushed it over OTA, then checked the old placeholder password got rejected and the new one got accepted. One false "heartbeat DOWN" from Kuma went out while the old firmware was still running, which fair enough, it wasn't sending real heartbeats. While I'm on secrets: esphome config prints your Discord webhook in full, because it ends up inside a lambda. Don't paste that output anywhere. Two false alarms that were actually right Once it was talking, it straight away said two things were DOWN: SSH on the NAS and the router's web page. Both were fine from my laptop. The board was right though. I'd plugged it into a router port that's on my IoT VLAN, so it got an IoT address. And my IoT VLAN isn't allowed to reach NAS SSH or the router's admin page. That's the firewall doing its job. I moved that router port over to the main LAN, bounced the port so it asked for a new address, and it picked up its reserved one. 10 out of 10 up, and it posted RECOVERED for both. Kuma's ping monitor for it went green too. Worth saying: a watchdog that sits on a different network from the thing it watches is testing the firewall, not the service. Put it where your users are. What I added after A password on its web page. sieve, my own vulnerability scanner, flagged the open web UI, so it's behind a login now. An off-site dead-man switch. The board can tell me a server is down, but if the power goes or the internet drops, nothing at home can tell me anything. So I've got a free Cloudflare Worker that expects check-ins and posts to Discord if they stop for 5 minutes. Two of my servers already pinged it every minute, and since 16 October the watchdog does too, every cycle. That one's got its own story (the cron trigger didn't fire at first), I'll write it up separately. How it's doing This is the board's own state, read off its web page on 18 October 2026: 2,061 check cycles, about 34 hours since its last restart, nothing down, nothing stuck in the queue. Not much to look at, which is the point. If you're building one On a production ESP32-P4, use variant: esp32p4 and engineering_sample: false, not the evboard. In ESPHome C++ code, call ::socket and friends with the :: in front. Check something real for DNS, not just the port. Put the board on the same network as whoever uses the services, or you're testing the firewall. Have something off-site for the power cut case, because the board goes off with everything else. What watches your monitoring? I genuinely didn't have an answer to that until this month. 🤖 Drafted with AI assistance from my own homelab notes, logs and repos, and fact-checked against them before publishing.

articles.title: Two Agents, Two Definitions of 'Done': The Contract to Write Before You Wire Them Together
articles.description: The failure mode nobody writes about: two AI agents, both running, both "up" on every dashboard — and the job quietly not getting done. On the November 11 episode of The Cognitive Revolution, Vijoy Pandey — SVP and GM of Outshift by Cisco, the incubation arm that has deployed multi-agent systems with Swisscom, ServiceNow, SoftServe, and Webex — described a gap that standard monitoring never shows. In Cisco's own five-agent deployments, accuracy fell from 99% with no misalignments between the agents to 16% with three. In one travel-booking test, the system was mostly up and connected while completing zero tasks. And in an analysis of public ChatDev sessions, Cisco reported semantic or cognitive-misalignment failures in 100% of the sessions it examined. "Connectivity is not the same as cognition," Pandey told host Nathan Labenz. "What we need to move towards is shared cognition and shared reasoning." His diagnosis: the industry measures whether agents are up and connected, while agents can be connected and still not understand each other. The value, he argued, is not in any one agent — "the value is actually in the handoff that's happening between these agents." The failure isn't capability. It's vocabulary. Most multi-agent advice focuses on architecture: which agent does what, who orchestrates, how they connect. The failure Pandey described is duller and more dangerous: two competent agents that mean different things by the same word. At small-business scale, the version looks like this: Your sales agent marks a job "done" when the customer accepts the quote. Your invoicing agent considers the job "done" when payment clears. Your sales agent calls someone a "customer" the moment they sign. Your billing system calls them a "customer" only once an invoice exists. Both definitions are defensible. Neither agent is broken. But the moment you wire automation across that seam — sales closes the job, invoicing starts billing — you have two different meanings of the trigger word routing real money. The handoff fires early, or late, or on the wrong population, and everything looks green while it happens. Cisco's answer was to open-source three protocols, which Outshift describes as observe, align, and validate: Scope builds knowledge graphs on agent traces to find cognitive failures; Accord has agents agree on intent, scope, key terms, and the definition of "done" before work starts; Concord has agents negotiate an outcome every one can accept when they disagree. You do not need to install any of that. You need the idea underneath it: the definitions get written down before the wiring, not after the failure. The handoff contract: one page, 20 minutes Before you connect any two agents — or an agent to a system it will trigger — write five fields. One page per seam; a three-agent setup has three seams, and each gets its own page. 1. Name the pair. "Sales agent → invoicing agent." Every contract covers exactly two systems. If a diagram is forming in your head, you're overcomplicating it — the contract is pairwise, not a hub. 2. List the words that cross the seam. Not every word — the load-bearing nouns, usually five or fewer: done, customer, paid, urgent, late. Pull the actual messages that will pass between the two systems and highlight the words both sides will act on. 3. Write each side's current definition. One line each, no editing, no fixing yet. Done (sales agent): quote accepted, kickoff email sent. Done (invoicing agent): invoice issued, payment reconciled. The differences are usually obvious the moment they're on paper — which is exactly why they need to be on paper. 4. Negotiate the shared definition. Where the two sides differ, write the one definition both will use — and make it checkable. "Done = quote accepted AND kickoff email sent AND invoice issued" is a definition an agent can test. "Done = the customer is taken care of" is a vibe. This is Accord's job shrunk to a paragraph. 5. Write the conflict rule. When a message arrives that doesn't fit the shared definitions, the receiving agent stops and asks a human. Never improvise a meaning. This is Concord's negotiation step shrunk to its SMB version: escalate, don't guess. The 99%-to-16% collapse came from misalignments that went uncorrected — the contract's job is to catch the collision while it's still a question, not a loss. Then run one real past case through the seam before you turn the wiring on — the trickiest one from last month. If the two agents don't classify it identically against the contract, the contract isn't finished. Where this fails (the honest list) A contract fixes collisions, not competence. Perfect definitions make two agents agree; they don't make either one good. If the model writes a bad email, the contract just ensures both agents agree it was sent. Sometimes the answer is one agent. If a single agent can do the whole job end to end, do that and skip the seam entirely. Contracts are for handoffs you actually need — don't create a second agent just to have something to wire. The numbers are a warning, not a benchmark. The 99%-to-16% collapse and the 100% ChatDev figure come from Cisco's own deployments and its analysis of public sessions. They establish the failure mode exists, not your odds of hitting it. Even the builders haven't finished. Pandey reported on the same episode that his own personal agent and his wife's — each carrying one identity across several models — still struggle to coordinate on their humans' behalf, down to booking a shared dinner. If the executive open-sourcing alignment protocols is still working on it, a one-page contract doesn't put you behind. It puts you ahead of most of the market. Where to start You can't write a handoff contract for agents you don't know you're running. Shadow usage means most small businesses already have two AI tools touching the same customers without anyone writing down what happens between them — one paid by the company, one installed by an employee, no shared definitions anywhere. That's the first thing the AI Clarity Sprint maps: every AI touchpoint in your business — paid tools, AI features inside software you already own, and the employee shadow usage nobody approved — in two weeks, for one fixed fee ($1,495 CAD). You finish with the complete inventory, the seams worth writing contracts for, and a ranked plan for what to do first. The cheapest place to fix a misalignment is before the wiring. The second cheapest is the week you find the seam.

articles.title: Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs: the flash chip attack on TPM lockout
articles.description: Originally published at coinetic.io. A short PIN is safe on Windows for one reason: after a few wrong guesses the TPM security chip makes you wait, so nobody can try all 10,000 four-digit PINs. Researchers at TU Berlin have shown that on some PCs this waiting can be undone by someone who opens the device and wires into the flash chip on the mainboard. This page explains what that means for your laptop, and the few settings that make it far harder. Why now: the "Hello Again" research (November 2026) What: the TPM in many PCs is built into the processor's firmware (a firmware TPM) and keeps its state, including the count of wrong PINs, in a flash chip on the mainboard. The researchers found that a Winbond flash chip can be made to leak its key by voltage glitching, and that AMD's firmware did not check that the counter in the flash really went up. Together this lets an attacker roll the TPM state back and keep guessing. Effect, per the paper: worst case for a 4-digit Windows Hello PIN drops from about 69 days to about 40 hours; for a 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN (TPM + PIN) from about 19 years to about 20 days. Longer PINs remain out of reach for practical purposes. Needs: the device itself, opened, with hardware attached to the mainboard. It is not a remote attack. No attacks outside the research lab were known at publication. Vendors: AMD tracks its part as CVE-2026-43613 (bulletin AMD-SB-7079) and is shipping firmware updates for affected processors from November 2026 into February 2027. According to reports, Microsoft rated the Windows Hello report moderate, did not assign a Windows CVE and recommends PINs of at least six digits; Intel says the flash chip used is the deciding factor; Winbond says a fix needs a new chip design. Sources: Research paper "Hello Again" (TU Berlin) · AMD security bulletin AMD-SB-7079 · Born's Tech and Windows World (German) In short Install firmware (BIOS / UEFI) updates from your PC maker as they arrive – that is where AMD's fix comes from, not from Windows Update alone. Make the PIN longer: at least 8 digits, or letters and digits. Every extra digit multiplies the attacker's work by ten. For BitLocker with a startup PIN: allow enhanced (alphanumeric) PINs and set a longer minimum length. Keep the device with you, and have a plan for a lost or stolen laptop: who to tell, which accounts to lock, which access to revoke. A firewall cannot stop a physical attack on a stolen laptop. It can keep your other computers from being opened with what is on that laptop. 1. What the attack does – in plain words Your Windows Hello PIN is not a password the attacker can test on another computer. It only works on this device, and the TPM chip counts wrong guesses and locks for a while after too many. That lockout is what makes a 4-digit PIN acceptable. The attack does not break the PIN or the encryption. It cheats the counter: the attacker saves the TPM's state from the flash chip, tries a few PINs, then puts the old state back so the TPM "forgets" the wrong guesses. Repeat until the PIN is found. With the PIN, the attacker can sign in to that laptop as you, use the keys Windows Hello protects (for example single sign-on to your company's cloud services from that device), and with a BitLocker startup PIN, unlock the disk. What it needs: your laptop, a screwdriver, soldering or clip-on wiring to the flash chip, and time – hours to days for a short PIN. This is a risk for a stolen or seized device, not for a PC that stays in your hands. 2. Is my PC affected? The research targets firmware TPMs that keep their state in the mainboard flash: AMD systems, and PCs with Winbond flash chips of the type examined, whatever the processor. Whether a given model is affected depends on processor and flash chip – watch your PC maker's security advisories. See which TPM you have: press Windows+R, type tpm.msc, Enter, and look at Manufacturer Name. Or in PowerShell: Get-Tpm | Select-Object ManufacturerIdTxt, ManufacturerVersion. AMD means the firmware TPM of an AMD processor. Desktops in a locked office are a smaller concern than laptops that travel. Rank by how easily a device can be taken away. 3. Updates first Firmware updates: AMD delivers its fix in processor firmware, which reaches you as a BIOS / UEFI update from your PC maker (HP, Lenovo, Dell, Framework and others). Use the maker's update tool or Windows Update's optional driver and firmware updates. Managed fleets: check your maker's advisory list for the models you own. Windows updates as usual. The firmware update does not replace a longer PIN: the research also covers flash chips for which no software fix exists. 4. Make the PIN longer The lockout was the only thing protecting short PINs. Without it, length is what counts. The researchers recommend adding at least two digits, or using eight or more. On your own PC Settings › Accounts › Sign-in options › PIN (Windows Hello) › Change PIN. Choose at least 8 digits – or tick Include letters and symbols, which makes guessing many times harder. In a company (Group Policy or Intune) Windows Hello PIN: Computer Configuration › Administrative Templates › System › PIN Complexity › Minimum PIN length (with newer templates also under Windows Components › Windows Hello for Business). Set at least 6, better 8. In Intune: Endpoint security › Account protection, or the Windows Hello for Business settings in the enrollment policy. Check after the rollout that users really have changed short PINs. BitLocker startup PIN: Computer Configuration › Administrative Templates › Windows Components › BitLocker Drive Encryption › Operating System Drives: Allow enhanced PINs for startup (letters and symbols) and Configure minimum PIN length for startup. Users then change their PIN with manage-bde -changepin C: as administrator. 5. Second-line defences for a lost or stolen device Report and revoke quickly: the attack takes time. If a laptop is missing, disable or delete the device in Entra ID / Intune, revoke the user's sessions, rotate the BitLocker recovery key, and reset the user's password. At home: change the password of your Microsoft account and sign out other devices from it. Remote wipe where you use Intune or another device management: a wiped device has nothing left to unlock. Do not rely on the device alone for access to important systems: require multi-factor sign-in with a second device (phone, security key) for VPN, remote access and admin accounts. Physical care: do not leave laptops in cars or hotel rooms; tamper-evident seals help notice an opened case. 6. What Coinetic AI Security can and cannot do here Honestly first: Coinetic AI Security manages the Windows Firewall. A firewall does not stop someone who has your laptop on their desk and wires into its mainboard, and Coinetic AI Security does not fix CVE-2026-43613. What Coinetic AI Security can do is make sure that a stolen laptop – or a stolen PIN – is not a key to your other computers over the internet: Phone unlock (Device approval): Remote Desktop, or any port you choose, stays invisible to the internet until you unlock it from your registered phone, for a set number of hours, and only for the address your phone is on. Every unlock is signed by your phone's passkey. Someone with your laptop and its saved Remote Desktop connections still finds nothing to connect to – unless they also have your unlocked phone. From your LAN and over a VPN, RDP keeps working. Details: Secure RDP without VPN. Lost phone? Block it: blocking or deleting a phone in Coinetic AI Security closes everything it opened at once. articles.title: Dev log #2: nationwide data, typo-proof search, and a subway bug that picked a train 2 hours later
articles.description: A follow-up to my first post. I'm an 11th grader in Korea building OWN SHARK solo: an assistant that tells you what's open near you, ranked by real walking time. Here's what landed in the last three days. The subway bug: answering with a train 2 hours later For subway legs I call Seoul Metro's shortest-path API. I only asked for the "shortest travel time" search type. Sometimes the shortest ride was a train leaving two hours from now, so the app proudly recommended it. The fix: ask all three search types (duration, fewest transfers, distance) for the time you'd actually reach the station, then keep whichever arrives first. Wait time for the first train is added in, and if it's over 10 minutes the reply says so. If the API has no answer, the app says the ride time isn't confirmed instead of guessing. From Seoul to the whole country Places, place names and addresses now cover all of Korea. The government business list is fetched per province every week, with a checkpoint per page so a dropped connection resumes where it stopped. A run that comes back with less than half the previous rows is refused rather than wiping data. Typo-proof name search SQLite FTS5 trigram indexes over place names. A one-syllable typo still finds the school, and you can type only the initial consonants (초성, e.g. "ㄱㄴㅇ"). Exact matches always rank above fuzzy ones. The big indexes are built by a startup job, never inside a request. Closing shops that shut down Shop records are matched to the government business-licence data, but only when the building and the name both match. If the licence says closed, the shop is closed. If more than 5% of one category would flip in a single run, nothing changes and the run is flagged for a human. For visitors Answers in Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese, not only Korean and English Incheon Airport: taxi stands, airport buses, gates, and live departure-hall queues from the airport's own API A paperwork-deadline helper for foreign residents, built from the immigration statute text; every answer cites the article and points to the official 1345 hotline Smaller things A 3D walking view: three.js buildings and a route ribbon inside MapLibre "Text mom I'm running late" opens the SMS screen with the text filled in. The user presses send A per-user monthly AI cost cap. Past it, the assistant falls back to rule-based answers Biggest lesson this round: don't take one API's answer as the truth. Both the subway bug and the closed shops were fixed by checking against a second source. Still pre-launch. Feedback very welcome. articles.title: What I learned building 700+ browser-only tools (no uploads, ever)
articles.description: I run theomnikit.com, a free site with 700+ small tools: PDF, image, video, developer utilities and calculators. Every file tool runs in the visitor's browser. Nothing is uploaded, and that one rule decided most of the engineering. This is what I learned getting there, including the parts that broke. I wrote this with AI help and checked every claim against the code and the project's decision log. The rule, and how it is enforced The first architecture decision was "browser-only; any server-side processing needs a new decision". A rule in a doc is easy to break quietly, so it is enforced by a test: no API route accepts a file (no multipart parser, no upload interceptor); nginx refuses any request body over 1 MB; the API's JSON parser stops at 1 MB. There is exactly one exception, and it has its own written decision: a screenshot attached to a bug report, redrawn on a canvas into a JPEG of at most 600 KB, so camera and location metadata never leave the device. One thing I got wrong early: I listed OCR as "out of scope" because I assumed it needed a server. It was the upload I had ruled out, not the reading of text. Image to Text now runs tesseract.js as WebAssembly. Because the CSP is connect-src 'self' and every Tesseract default points at a CDN, the worker, cores and language files are served from our own domain. How a file tool actually works The flow is the same everywhere: the File API hands over the bytes, the format is detected from the bytes (not the extension), the heavy library is fetched as soon as the file arrives, and the job runs when the person taps one button that names the action. Long jobs go to a Web Worker. The PDF tools, such as Grayscale PDF, share a small runner: one worker per tool, created on first use, the ArrayBuffer transferred rather than copied, progress posted back, and a fallback to the main thread when a worker cannot start. Workers are also a safety valve. The Regex Tester builds its worker from the same function the unit tests cover, and terminates it after 2 seconds, because a pattern that needs longer is almost always backtracking catastrophically. But a worker is not a fix for a bad algorithm. The diff checker froze on large inputs; moving it to a worker would have stopped the freeze and still failed the same comparisons. It got a better alignment algorithm with a time budget instead. Video without ffmpeg.wasm Video was where browser-only nearly broke. Single-threaded ffmpeg.wasm re-encoded a 5-minute 1080p video in 35 to 90 minutes. The multithreaded build needs SharedArrayBuffer, which means COOP/COEP headers, which blank out third-party ads, so that was not an option for a free site. The video tools, like Trim Video, use WebCodecs with mp4box and mp4-muxer instead: about 50 KB gzipped against ffmpeg's 32 MB. Trimming copies the original frames when the shape stays the same, so a short clip finishes in under a second with no quality loss. The pitfalls nobody warns you about iOS Safari's canvas limit. Safari refuses a canvas over about 16.7 megapixels, and recent iPhones shoot 24 MP by default. The failure is not even consistent: sometimes no context, sometimes an InvalidStateError on encode. Image to PDF now caps every encode at 16.7 MP, retries at half the pixels down to 2 MP, and tries a DOM canvas when OffscreenCanvas refuses. Thumbnails are full photos. Forty 12 MP photos in a preview strip is about 2 GB of decoded pixels on a phone. Thumbnails are now 480 px JPEGs made when the file is added. HEIC. One image tool accepted HEIC and handed it straight to createImageBitmap, so every HEIC failed in Chrome and Firefox, which cannot decode it. The image tools now share one loader that handles HEIC, and HEIC to JPG decodes with a dedicated library in the browser. Memory on big files. Before decoding an image, a pixel guard reads width and height from the first 256 KB and refuses an oversized image with a clear message. Running out of memory is reported as "too large for this browser", never as "damaged file", because it says nothing about the file. PDF limits, such as on Compress PDF, were deliberately not raised until browser memory is actually measured. Feature probes that lie. Every "to WebP" page once told visitors their browser could not write WebP, in a browser that could. The probe encoded a 1x1 OffscreenCanvas that had never had a rendering context, and that throws for every format. Test the probe, not just the feature. Why every tool is its own page Each tool has its own URL, title, short answer at the top and structured data, because the site has no marketing budget: people arrive from search engines and AI assistants asking one specific question, and the page has to be the answer. That also has a limit. Of 151 landing variants Google left "discovered, not indexed", 108 were folded into their parent with a 301. One page per real search intent, not one per keyword. State lives in the URL too. When one tool suggests the next step (say, compress the PDF you just made), the plan travels as link parameters, and the file is handed over in memory. No account, no server-side history. The standard that ties it together The bar for a file tool is two taps on a phone: choose the file, confirm. Zero scrolls. The site never runs a job on a dropped file by itself; that one confirmation is what makes "your files never leave your device" believable. If you are building something similar: write the no-upload rule down, enforce it with a test, put long jobs in workers, and test on a real iPhone early. Most of my bugs were in that last one.

articles.title: Part 32: Data residency and on-prem runtimes compared
articles.description: Part 32 · One Agent, Five Platforms Regulated? Then where the agent and its data run matters as much as what it does. An invoice agent reads supplier bank details, approval history and amounts. A security or data protection review will ask three questions before it asks anything about prompts: Runtime: where does the agent itself run, and can it run in our own infrastructure? Model: where are prompts and completions processed? Logs: where do traces, conversation history and audit records end up? Part 30 flagged residency as the control with the most gaps. This part answers the three questions for each platform, from vendor documentation I read on 20 November 2026. Like the builds, it's documentation-only, and the gaps are stated rather than filled. MuleSoft Runtime. Agent networks deploy to a CloudHub 2.0 shared or private space, or a Runtime Fabric target. Runtime Fabric runs on infrastructure you manage, so it's the customer-hosted option (Part 11). The control planes overview lists agent network projects and the LLM gateway as available on the EU control plane. Since 16 November 2026, the release notes also list Hyperforce as a target for version 2.0 agent networks. Model. The broker calls an LLM provider you configure, through the gateway. I found no statement about where those calls are processed. That depends on the provider and region you choose. Logs. Traces and logs go to Anypoint Monitoring, and the EU control plane lists log search, raw log data and a telemetry exporter. Retention and storage location weren't on the pages I read. Boomi Runtime. The runtime clouds page lists four Boomi-managed clouds: US East, UK, Japan and Australia. There's still no EU cloud; the UK one is outside the EU. A self-hosted Flex runtime "runs in your own infrastructure" but is in early access, as it was in Part 15. Model. The Boomi AI FAQ says agents use models through Amazon Bedrock, and that each runtime runs the model, prompts and responses "in the selected region". You can also connect your own Anthropic, OpenAI or Google account, in which case prompts go to that provider. On Flex, "only the model prompt leaves your network". Logs. Audit trace logs are in Agent Control Tower, without a stated retention period. Chat sessions are kept until a user deletes them. Two exceptions matter for residency: glossary and knowledge base content is stored in the platform's region, so a North America customer running agents in the UK, Japan or Australia retrieves it from the US. SAP Runtime. The Business AI reference architecture says the platform is "SAP-managed by default", with SAP AI Core running on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. SAP Learning's data residency lesson describes locally hosted AI, SAP Sovereign Cloud and an EU AI Cloud with "AI infrastructure hosted within Europe". I found no on-premises option for Joule agents, and no availability dates for those offerings. Model. Models come through the generative AI hub, from SAP and partners such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and Cohere. The lesson says processing "may occur on SAP-managed infrastructure or approved external model providers, depending on the use case and configuration". I found no way to pin Joule's model calls to a region. Logs. Not covered in what I read, as in Part 18. The architecture mentions agent session telemetry going to SAP Cloud ALM, but not where it's stored or for how long. Azure Runtime. Foundry Agent Service endpoints are regional, and the FAQ says "data is stored in the same region as the endpoint". In the standard setup, threads, files and vector stores go to your own Cosmos DB, Storage and AI Search resources. Agents can run in your virtual network, on a delegated subnet in the same region. There's no on-premises option on these pages. Model. This is where Azure is clearest. The deployment types page defines three levels: Global: may be processed in any Azure region. Data Zone: processed only within the US, EU or APAC zone. The EU zone is the EU Data Boundary. Standard (regional): processed within the geography you choose. In every case, "data stored at rest remains in the designated Azure geography". So the deployment type you pick is a residency decision, not just a pricing one. Logs. Traces go to an Application Insights resource in your own subscription (Part 22). AWS Runtime. AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Identity and Observability are available in seven European regions, according to the regions page: Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain and Stockholm. Milan and Spain don't have Memory or Runtime Instances yet. The runtime can attach to your VPC (Part 25). There's no on-premises option. Model. Bedrock's geographic cross-Region inference keeps EU requests within EU regions. But prompts and results "might move outside of your source Region", and any abuse-detection copies are stored in the destination region. On the AgentCore side, the cross-Region inference page says Memory, Policy and Evaluations use it. From the EU regions it stays in Europe. From some other source regions, Policy and Evaluations use global routing that can leave the geography. Logs. Observability writes to CloudWatch in your account (Part 25). The cross-Region page warns that CloudWatch and CloudTrail logs "won't specify the AWS Region in which data inference occurs". What the builds could and could not show Could: where each vendor says the runtime runs, which regions exist, and which platforms offer a customer-hosted runtime. MuleSoft has Runtime Fabric, and Boomi has Flex in early access. Could not: where model calls actually land for MuleSoft and SAP, and log retention on most of them. Those need the vendor's trust documentation or contract terms, and a hands-on build that checks the traces. For an EU-only requirement: Azure's Data Zone and AWS's EU regions are the most explicit in the docs. MuleSoft can keep the runtime and control plane in the EU but leaves model location to your provider. Boomi has no EU-managed cloud. SAP describes an EU AI Cloud without dates I could find. The policy from Part 30 still holds: classify the data first, then pick the runtime, model deployment and log store that keep each class where it's allowed. Where must your agent data stay? This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. This part is based only on vendor documentation read on 20 November 2026 and the documentation-only builds in Parts 11 to 30; no hands-on build has been run yet. It's not legal or compliance advice. Views are my own.

articles.title: Healthtech Background Job Queue: Fixing Malformed 256KB JSON Payloads
articles.description: Short answer: keep the renewal command small, validate the serialized bytes and schema in both the Node.js producer and consumer, and store the large health record outside the queue behind a stable reference. The 256 KB ceiling is a contract boundary, not a retryable incident; malformed JSON and schema failures should be quarantined with an audit record, while a delayed reminder should be recoverable through idempotent consumer state. This matters when a healthtech business wants to delay a renewal reminder until a contract or business deadline. The reminder is time-sensitive, but its payload should not become a copy of the subscription, patient, or billing aggregate. A queue message should say what must happen, when the decision was made, and where the worker can obtain the minimum authorized input. How should a background job queue reject malformed 256KB payloads? Treat the producer and consumer as two independent contract boundaries. The producer creates an explicit envelope, serializes it once, measures the resulting byte length, and refuses a message above 256 KB. The consumer performs the same byte check before parsing, then parses JSON, validates the schema, checks domain rules, and only then starts the reminder workflow. Repeating validation is deliberate: a delayed message may outlive a deployment, and another publishing path may not share the producer's assumptions. The order prevents confusing failures. A byte-limit violation is not a JSON parse error. A malformed document is not a schema violation. A syntactically valid object can still lack a message ID, a deadline, a schema version, or the reference needed to decide whether a reminder is still appropriate. Log those classifications separately; otherwise an operations dashboard will describe three different contract failures as one mysterious retry spike. The practical envelope for this scenario is small: type RenewalReminder struct { SchemaVersion int `json:"schema_version"` MessageID string `json:"message_id"` AccountID string `json:"account_id"` Deadline string `json:"business_deadline"` Subscription string `json:"subscription_ref"` Template string `json:"template_version"` } The reference is not automatically harmless. In a healthtech system, an account ID or subscription reference can still be personal data, so it belongs in the deletion inventory and access-control model. GDPR Article 17 does not stop applying because the identifier moved from an HTTP request into a queue or a database table. The architecture decision record: where does recovery stop? The decision is to use a versioned command envelope, a durable inbox, and a separate source for large objects. The invariants are more important than the queue brand: A message is accepted only if its serialized bytes are at or below 256 KB. The schema version, command identity, business deadline, and reference are required. The consumer records the message ID before the reminder side effect, using a uniqueness constraint in the same transaction as the business state transition. An acknowledgement follows the committed transaction, not the moment the worker begins processing. A permanent contract failure is recorded and quarantined; a transient delivery failure can be retried within a bounded policy. This is an exactly-once mindset applied where it can actually be enforced. A queue may deliver a message more than once. The application can still make the business effect happen once by putting the inbox insert and the reminder-state update in one database transaction. If the worker crashes after the transaction commits but before acknowledgement, redelivery finds the existing message ID and does not send a second reminder. The audit row should include the message ID, schema version, correlation ID, disposition, timestamp, and a digest of the received bytes. It generally should not include the raw health record or the entire JSON body. A digest lets an investigator connect a repeated failure to an input without spreading another copy of regulated data through logs. Recovery becomes much clearer when the producer's refusal and the consumer's quarantine are treated as different observations. A producer can reject a message before it leaves the application, which is the cheapest place to expose a growing payload and the best place to return a useful validation error to the caller. A consumer, by contrast, has to assume that the message may have been emitted by an older release, replayed from a redrive tool, or produced by a second service that did not share the current schema package. It therefore records what it actually received, including the byte count and digest, rather than copying the producer's explanation. During an investigation, those two records answer different questions: did the publishing path understand the contract, and did the worker enforce the contract at the point of side effect? Keeping both answers makes an audit trail useful without making the queue a second patient-record system. It also gives an operator a controlled repair path: correct the producer, deploy the schema change, inspect quarantined IDs, and redrive only messages whose business deadlines and authorization still make them valid. Keep it boring. Decision area Compact command envelope Full aggregate in the message Size control Easy to measure before publish Can cross 256 KB as fields grow Schema change Versioned command contract Couples the worker to unrelated fields Privacy Keeps routine copies out of the queue Replicates sensitive fields into queue retention Recovery Redrive one command after fixing the cause Reconstruct and re-authorize a large object Appropriate use Renewal decision and stable reference A small, self-contained, non-sensitive object The rejected option is compression as the primary fix. Compression may reduce transport bytes, but it does not solve schema coupling, retention, access control, or a consumer that parses an unexpected version. Fragmenting one large object is worse for recovery: now operators must reconcile missing pieces, duplicate fragments, ordering, expiration, and authorization at assembly time. There is a valid use for the full-object design. Use it when the object is demonstrably below the limit, has a stable versioned schema, contains no separately governed data, and has idempotent processing. That is a reasonable choice for a compact internal command. It is a poor default for an evolving healthtech aggregate. A Go reference implementation for the producer-consumer boundary The following sample shows the critical path without pretending that an in-memory map is a production inbox. The production version should put the uniqueness check, renewal-state change, and outbox or send decision under the database's transaction rules. The sample's useful property is its failure classification: oversize, malformed JSON, and invalid schema do not enter an endless retry loop. package main import ( "crypto/sha256" "encoding/hex" "encoding/json" "errors" "fmt" ) func validate(job RenewalReminder) error { if job. SchemaVersion != 1 { return fmt. Errorf("unsupported schema version: %d", job. SchemaVersion) if job. MessageID == "" || job. AccountID == "" || job. Deadline == "" || job. Subscription == "" || job. Template == "" { return errors. New("message_id, account_id, deadline, subscription_ref, and template_version are required") return nil func encodeForPublish(job RenewalReminder) ([]byte, error) { if err := validate(job); err != nil { return nil, fmt. Errorf("schema rejected before publish: %w", err) payload, err := json. Marshal(job) if err != nil { return nil, fmt. Errorf("JSON encoding failed: %w", err) if len(payload) > maxMessageBytes { return nil, fmt. Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes) return payload, nil func consume(payload []byte, inbox map[string]string) error { return fmt. Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes) var job RenewalReminder if err := json. Unmarshal(payload, &job); err != nil { return fmt. Errorf("permanent JSON failure: %w", err) return fmt. Errorf("permanent schema failure: %w", err) if priorDigest, exists := inbox[job. MessageID]; exists { digest := sha256. Sum256(payload) inbox[job. MessageID] = hex. EncodeToString(digest[:]) func main() { job := RenewalReminder{ SchemaVersion: 1, MessageID: "renewal-20260811-001", AccountID: "acct-4821", Deadline: "2026-08-15T17:00:00Z", Subscription: "sub-2048", Template: "renewal-v3", payload, err := encodeForPublish(job) panic(err) inbox := map[string]string{} if err := consume(payload, inbox); err != nil { The real Node.js implementation should preserve the same sequence even if its validation library differs: use a byte measurement of the encoded Buffer, not a character count; reject unknown schema versions; and keep the producer's error response distinct from the consumer's quarantine disposition. A JavaScript string length is not a reliable proxy for UTF-8 bytes when the payload contains non-ASCII data. One subtle healthtech rule belongs after validation but before sending: re-read the subscription state and compare it with the stored deadline and template policy. A renewal can be cancelled, paid, or moved while the message waits. The worker should record that decision as a normal terminal disposition, not send an old reminder because the queue message was technically valid. How can operators distinguish retryable delivery failures from contract failures? Use a small state machine rather than one generic failed flag. published means the producer passed local validation. received means the consumer obtained bytes. quarantined means the bytes or schema cannot produce a valid command. ready means the inbox transaction committed and the reminder is eligible for the deadline policy. sent means the external notification outcome was recorded. A separate cancelled or superseded state handles a subscription that changed while work was waiting. The retry rule follows the state, not the emotional urgency of the reminder. A broker connection interruption, temporary database unavailability, or notification provider timeout may be retriable with a finite attempt budget. Invalid JSON, an unsupported schema version, a missing reference, and a 256 KB violation are deterministic; retrying them creates noise and can delay valid work behind a poisoned message. A dead-letter or quarantine record should retain the message ID, error class, schema version if parseable, byte count, digest, and the producer release identifier. RabbitMQ's consumer acknowledgement documentation is useful here because acknowledgement timing is an explicit part of delivery semantics. A worker should acknowledge after durable application state is committed, and it should expect redelivery when the process ends before acknowledgement. The acknowledgement is not an audit record and cannot substitute for an inbox constraint. For a delayed reminder, recovery also requires visibility into time. Measure queue age, time until business deadline, quarantine count by error class, redelivery count, inbox duplicates, and the number of reminders superseded before sending. Alert on a deadline approaching with no ready state, not only on worker crashes. A healthy process can repeatedly reject every message and still look green if the only metric is process uptime. I once assumed the parse-error rate was the important signal in this class of system. It wasn't. The more useful question was how many valid reminders had less than an hour before their business deadline while waiting behind invalid work. That metric changed the recovery conversation from “the queue is noisy” to “these 18 accounts need an operator decision.” When is a different queue architecture the right choice? The compact command pattern is not a universal answer. A queue is a poor source of truth for compliance evidence, and a short retention window is not a replay archive. If the business requires long-lived event replay, independent consumer groups, or historical reconstruction, use an event-log design with explicit retention and deletion controls. If the workflow has many durable steps, timers, joins, or human approvals, a workflow engine may express recovery more clearly than a hand-built retry table. Stay with a simple queue when the job is one bounded command, the consumer owns an idempotency boundary, and operators can redrive quarantined messages after correcting the producer. Choose a workflow or event-log architecture when recovery requires reconstructing a sequence rather than repeating one command. The catch is operational ownership: each broader model adds retention, replay, permissions, and audit decisions that the team must test and document. The final decision rule is narrow. Put only the renewal intent and a controlled reference on the queue; make byte size and schema validation executable at both ends; commit idempotent state before acknowledgement; and keep compliance evidence in a durable system designed for audit and erasure. That's enough architecture to make a 256 KB failure boring, which is exactly what an operator needs at a business deadline.
